Mr. H. H. STEVENS (Centre Vancouver) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 41, to amend the Railway Act.
He said: Very briefly, the object of this Bill is to amend certain sections of the Railway Act in which reference is made to the matter of discrimination in rates. In the Act as it now stands the word

"discrimination" is invariably preceded by words such as "unreasonable", "undue", "unfair", and such like. This Bill proposes to remove these words, thus making the question of discrimination an absolute one, rather than one that is subject to these modifications.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOSEPH ARCHAMBAULT (Cham-bly and Vercheres) moved:
speechtext:
Whereas, the regulations of the Department of Agriculture provide, in connection with autumn shows of domestic animals and poultry, that agricultural societies which have spent a minimum amount of $3,600 of their own money in their preceding show for the granting of prizes to the above classes of exhibits, will be entitled to a minimum grant of $2,500 from the Department of Agriculture.
Whereas, in fixing a sum of $3,600 as a minimum of expenses for the obtention of a grant the department does not encourage in any way the small local fairs held in counties which as an average distribute about $500 in prizes for aforesaid classes of exhibits.
In the opinion of this House it is expedient to amend the present regulations by reducing the minimum to $500, and by entitling the said fairs to the two-thirds of the amount expended in the previous year, this fraction being given as a grant providing that the amount expended was at least $500.	^
He said: Mr. Speaker, the object of this resolution is apparent as the motion speaks for itself, and it is my intention to be very brief in the remarks which I purpose to make in support of it. In passing, I may remark that this is another non-partisan resolution. Its purpose is to encourage local and county exhibitions of domestic animals and poultry. As the lAgulations of the department now stand, it is provided that, in connection with the autumn shows of domestic animals and poultry, agricultural societies which have spent a minimum of $3,600 of their own money in their preceding show in the granting of prizes to the above classes of exhibits shall be entitled to a minimum grant of $2,500 from the Department of Agriculture. Now, there are no local or county shows of domestic animals and poultry which have ever spent as large an amount of $3,600 as a minimum for prizes, and I understand that this year the minimum has been raised by the minister to $4,000. I have a list here of the counties surrounding my district, with the respective sums distributed last year in prizes. In the

county of La Prairie the amount was $600.05; in the county of St. John, $441.25; in the county of Napierville, $414.50; in the county of Rouville, $597.20; in the county of Chambly, $741.45; and in the county of Vercheres, $801.
These regulations may be all right for provincial and regional exhibitions, but the fixing of a minimum of $3,600 or $4,000 altogether precludes the local or county exhibitions from any share of the grants made by the Federal Government to agricultural societies. To prove my contention, I may say that I am informed by the department that last year in Canada there were only twenty or twenty-one exhibitions or shows of the kind which got the Federal grant. In my province there were only five. These were the exhibitions at St. Scholastique, Sherbrooke, Three Rivers, Ormstown, and Quebec. The exhibition at St. Scholastique is a regional exhibition in which practically four, five, or six counties participate. At Sherbrooke it is an industrial exhibition, that place being a city. At Three Rivers it is the same. At Ormstown the show is a regional exhibition and at Quebec it is a provincial exhibition. I surmise that in the other provinces the same thing occurs- that no local or county exhibition of that kind ever gives prizes to an amount as high as the minimum fixed by the department.

Does the provincial
government of Quebec give grants to these smaller fairs on the basis of the prize money paid out?

The provincial government gives prizes but not on the basis of the prize money paid out. I believe the grants are given on the basis of the number of members belonging to each agricultural society' in the proportion of two dollars for one. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the Federal Government should also encourage these local and county exhibitions; I submit that they are much more deserving of support than are the regional or provincial exhibitions. My reason for making that statement is that: in the local and county shows a keen rivalry prevails between the exhibitors or farmers of the district or riding. They can go to these shows, compete against each other and have a chance to win prizes. At the regional or provincial exhibitions the awards are nearly always carried off some wealthy corporation or breeder possessing the means to purchase prize cattle and so secure the prizes. This is one of the reasons why the local shows should be encouraged.
Furthermore, the farmer of ordinary means will not exhibit at the regional or provincial shows because it means too much expense to him. These shows generally last five dr six days, and the farmer, if he wishes to exhibit at them, has in the first place to lose that period of time. Then he has to make provision for travelling expenses to the place of exhibition, which is generally situated at a distance from his farm. He has also to incur the expense involved during the five or six days that he is attending the exhibition. On the other hand the county fair, or the local show, is generally held at a place which is in the centre of the county and very close to the farmer's home, and it lasts but one day. The farmer gets up very early in the morning, goes to the local show, spends the whole day there and returns to his home the same night. I see my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) laughing, but .that is what happens in my county.
The farmer always gets up early.

That is true, but on the morning of the local exhibition he gets up even much earlier. As I said before, the local exhibitions should be encouraged to a greater extent than the regional or provincial shows because they result in much benefit to the farmer of ordinary means. Another reason for their encouragement is this: The regional or provincial shows require extensive buildings for exhibition purposes, while the county or local shows practically do not require buildings of any very great value. A still further reason for the encouragement of the county shows is because they are entirely agricultural in their character. You do not find at the local shows-at l&ast it is the case in the province of Quebec and I presume the same conditions prevail in the other provinces-"midway" attractions and shows which, if not of an immoral character are certainly vulgar, to say nothing of the crowd of fakirs, such as are witnessed at the provincial or regional exhibitions. Attractions of this kind very often deprive the farmers of their money, and they allure young people who would otherwise be examining the respective exhibits of the exhibition proper and deriving an educational advantage therefrom. The object of my resolution is not to do away with the grants to regional or provincial exhibitions, but simply to give more encouragement to the local and county shows. The only objection which

might be urged to its adoption, is that it would involve some additional expenditure. Well, out of the 235 counties or ridings in Canada there are about 54 urban constituencies, leaving 181 rural ridings. If I take $600 as the average amount of the prizes given in each county for these local shows, which would entitle the counties to get two-thirds, or $400, it would only involve an expenditure of $72,400. Even if I increased that average and placed it at $900, which is a pretty high figure for prizes for these shows, the two-thirds would amount to $600, and 181 counties at $600 would only represent a total of $108,600. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Agriculture' who is a practical man and has devoted himself with great earnestness towards promoting the welfare and development of agriculture, should agree to my resolution, for it would be a great boom for the agriculturists of this country and be decidedly to the advantage of the farming community.

I beg to support the motion of my hon. friend from Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault). The other day, when discussing the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, I pointed out to the minister at the head of that department the importance of stimulating the development of agriculture through the medium of these country fairs. In the county of Lotbiniere we have the good fortune of having one of the finest country fairs in our section of the province. We have a permanent building in which are exhibited every year the products of the farmers of the county, and it is encouraging to see the zeal which the farmers display and the keenness with which they compete for the prizes which are offered. But it is not possible to offer to these farmers in the one county the sum of $4,000 which is the minimum fixed by the Department of Agriculture entitling an exhibition to a grant. If this minimum were lowered to $500, as suggested by the resolution of my hon. friend from Chambly and Vercheres, these farmers could obtain from the department a grant which would materially assist them, and would be of greater benefit to the development of agriculture than are those regional exhibitions which, as my hon. friend has just said, are more of the character of a circus than of an agricultural fair. For this reason, Sir, I think that if the hon. minister can see his way clear to get the necessary money to encourage these country fairs, he will advance IMr. Archambault.]
the interests of agriculture in a most practical way.
I do not wish to repeat what I said to the Minister of Agriculture the other day when discussing his Estimates, but I can assure him that I give my heartiest support to the resolution. And I cordially invite him to attend the agricultural exhibition at Lotbiniere next September, when he will see the progressive character of the farming population in that district, and will be convinced, I think, that the grants will be convinced, I think, that his grants have been taken full advantage of.
Mr. EMMANUEL D'ANJOU (Rimou-ski) : (Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a word in support of the motion introduced by the hon. member for Cham-bly-Vercheres (Mr. Archambault). It is certainly one of the most interesting resolutions which have been submitted to the House during the present session.
I would not like to hurt the feelings of my hon. friend the member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien), but I believe that we have country fairs in Rimouski which are as fine as any in his country. Two years ago, in the county of Rimouski, county fairs were started, and all who have taken part in these agree in saying that most certainly there are none better. They are not a meeting place for amusement, a circus, they are only an exhibition of all the agricultural products which the farmers of the county may bring. If the motion introduced by the hon. member for Chambly-Verchdres were passed it would assuredly be an encouragement to our farmers who have such great sacrifices to make; such as loss of time and loss of money, in order to enter into competition in these fairs.
The district of Rimouski is certainly one of the important agricultural districts^ of the country, one of the most progressive. Our farmers are model farmers; they are attached to the earth and do their best in every circumstance to prove that they are experts in agriculture.
I do not wish to insist further, but I think that all the hon. members, and especially those who represent agricultural counties, should strongly support the resolution moved by the hon. member for Chambly-Vercheres and urge the Government to accept it. This would enhance the interest attaching to our country fairs, and besides, would encourage our agriculturists to increase production, which we so urgently need at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I think the general principle of this resolution, the principle of encouraging the production of better live stock, should be supported. But the function of this Parliament is not. provincial, and it seems to me that some duty falls upon the provincial authorities to encourage these smaller fairs. In the province of Ontario such fairs are encouraged by grants from the provincial government, based upon the amount of money paid out in prizes by the several fairs. It seems to me that the sponsor of this resolution should not expect the Federal Government to go any further than the provincial governments are prepared to go in assisting these smaller fairs. For my part, I would be prepared to support a motion to the effect that the Government contribute an amount equal to the amount given by the several provincial governments in the way of grants to these fairs.
A good deal can be said in favour of the hon. gentleman's statement that the larger fairs are patronized by the wealthy stock breeders who make a business of exhibiting prize animals. I have had some little experience in connection with the smaller fairs, haying been the secretary and manager of one for a number, of years, and I may say that some fairs are open to this criticism, that very often, because they are only one-day fairs, somebody will drive in every animal he has on his farm, whether he ought to be ashamed to exhibit them or not, for the sake of getting some kind of prize. Therefore, in connection with making grants to these fairs I think it should be stipulated that expert judges be engaged, especially as our agricultural colleges are providing us with first-class men who are available for these duties. If we are to pay out federal money to encourage the production of first-class stock, we should have judges who are capable of passing an expert opinion upon that stock, and not merely some local man who will award a prize to any grade of animal, no matter whether it is worthy of a prize or not. If animals are not up to a certain standard no prizes should be given. A conscientious judge drawn from the locality in which the fair is held will often exact that high standard, but I must say, speaking from my own experience, a local judge is more apt to be influenced by his friends in the neighbourhood and to say, "Well, this animal is not quite up to the standard, but we will give it a prize anyway." I do not believe that the indiscriminate awarding of prizes encourages the production of good stock. I am in favour of some help being given by the Dominion Government to encourage the breeding of good stock, but such help should be supplemented dollar for dollar by the provincial authorities.

Mr. Speaker, I share the opinion of other hon. members that our country fairs should be encouraged in every reasonable way. But I am afraid I cannot go so far as even the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) in saying that the Dominion should give grants to these smaller fairs, even as supplementary to the grants given by the provinces, These smaller fairs are purely provincial or local, and this House has about enough on its hands just now without branching out into anything of this kind. I cannot agree with the hon. gentleman who introduced the resolution that so small an amount as he suggests would be required. I think I could point to as many fairs in our province as he suggests altogether; many agricultural societies there would pay out from $500 to $1,000 in prizes if they could get two-thirds of it from the Dominion. In my constituency alone there are twelve or fourteen agricultural societies. Putting it at ten and multiplying that by say two hundred constituencies in Canada, you have two thousand fairs.
Does my hon. friend understand that we speak of one fair per riding and not of agricultural societies, of which we have a number in each riding?

I am dealing with the resolution as I find it. You may call them "fairs" or "autumn shows," whichever you like-" a rose by any other name would smell as sweet." I do not think the name has anything to do with it. We call them all "agricultural societies" in our country; and we do all that sort of work through these societies. I do not think the resolution is confined to one exhibition or show for each riding; I think it would be absurd to suggest that any one agricultural riding can support only one fair of that kind. I have a good deal more faith in the progressiveness of the farmers of Canada than to believe anything of that kind.
Now, we have our agricultural fairs in Saskatchewan, and to these the province gives some assistance, as do municipalities in many cases. We have no counties



in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, so my hon. friend's remark would not apply. We have rural municipalities, and they are disposed to treat fairly the smaller exhibitions. But even at that we find it very difficult to keep these exhibitions going, and I am very sorry that is the case, because I believe that the small agricultural exhibition properly handled is very beneficial to the country. But I do not think that this House or this Government should undertake, as finances are at the present time, to give assistance in cases of that kind. To do so would take not the small sum mentioned by my hon. friend, but in the neighbourhood of a . million dollars, if the thing is to be done properly. I do not think that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) has a million dollars at his disposal for any purpose of that kind. I do not want to discourage my hon. friend in his desire to secure the expenditure of money for the benefit of the farmers or in support of agricultural exhibitions or shows-he may call them what he likes. It is desirable that these smaller shows should be encouraged. However, I cannot join in the request that such an expenditure be made by the Dominion because, as I have said,
I do not think we should spend money in that way, at the present time, at least.

Mr. Speaker, I have a great deal of pleasure in supporting the principle of this resolution, and one of the reasons why I do so has just been mentioned by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson). That hon. gentleman says that the attendance at smaller fairs is falling away. This we all know to be the case. These small exhibition organizations have great difficulty in keeping up their prizes; and that is particularly true of all the small fairs, I think, in the province of Ontario. Many things contribute to this condition. The principal reason, I think, is found in the more general use of the automobile. Most farmers get into their cars and drive to the fair to see what their neighbours are exhibiting, while their neighbours, like themselves, have brought nothing, because it does not pay them to do so.
We know, too, that along with the progress of fairs has gone the development of ' stock. That is quite easily proved, especially in the new parts of the country where the small fall fairs are carried on. The improvement in the class of stock thus brought about is the result, largely, of competition; nothing will induce improvement [Mt. Thomson, Qu'Appelle],
in the class of stock like keen competition among neighbours in small municipalities. This does not apply to the same extent in the case of larger fairs, but if you want to improve the condition of the stock in the rural and backward parts of a province I do not know of any one thing more conducive to that end than to bring about an improvement of the calibre and the class of the fall fairs-an improvement which in itself hinges largely upon the extent of the prize list. In nearly all cases the prize list is too small to recompense a man for the trouble incidental to the exhibiting of his stock at a fair. I think, therefore, that if Parliament could see its way clear to grant -I would not say a few hundred thousand dollars; I would not restrict it to a million, because I think it would be an investment that would be productive of splendid returns to the people of this country-if, I say, we could spend a million or a million and a half along these lines, the results during the next five or ten years would be of an extremely beneficial character. I agree with the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) that anything of this kind must be worked out on a sound basis. His suggestion that the assistance to be given by the Dominion be based on the provincial grants, which, in turn, in the case of Ontario at least, are based on the amount contributed by the municipality, is a fair one. You there have some finality of responsibility; you there have a just basis upon which to build up your prize list. I do think that if this country is going to make progress and if it is to pay off its national debt, nothing will hold out such a favourable prospect in that direction as the development of our stock raising industry, and that, in turn, must be based upon the building up of higher grades of the different breeds of stock. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I have very much pleasure in supporting at least the principle of this resolution, and I hope that the minister may be able to carry into effect the substance of the suggestions incorporated in it.

Mr. Speaker, a short time ago, when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) had his Estimates before the House, at a late hour in the night we on this side, feeling that the minister had been kind enough to answer a good many questions, felt that we would like to give him a chance to pass a few items. Just about that time, Sir, he made the affirmation that in British Columbia a certain kind of hens had been

laying three hundred eggs per year. I take it that on a resolution of this kind, involving the discussion of exhibitions and fairs in connection with which poultry would he exhibited, we may fairly ask the minister to state to the House what kind of hens he was speaking about. I think everybody would be glad to know something more about hens that would lay three hundred eggs per year.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to add a few words to this discussion, now drawing to its termination, regarding the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archamhault). The object of our rural agricultural exhibitions seems to be somewhat ignored or to have gone out of sight. In our departments of agriculture, there seems to be a particular tendency to encourage poultry and cattle breeding, without taking into account the fact that agricultural exhibitions in rural districts include every one of the farm products. For instance, there is held in the district of Montmagny one of the largest country fairs in this Dominion, an exhibition that at times will last as long as three days.
The capital required for the buildings necessary for this exhibition is considerable. It is difficult to determine exactly what is the sum spent to encourage poultry and cattle breeding, and to separate it from the sum given in general as prizes for all agricultural products. The farmers who represent the mass of Canadian farmers, go in for general farming and do not specialize in any one branch. He really represents the national agricultural asset, and I believe, as was said just now by one of the hon. members on the right, that he deserves more attention than any other class of agriculturists. The one who goes in for stock-raising exclusively is usually a rich man who does not require the stimulus of these exhibitions to lead him to improve his products in quality and quantity. The large exhibitions which are now encouraged by the Department of Agriculture really serve almost any end, but that intended. The large breeders who show their animals at these exhibitions do so not so much to win prizes as to let other breeders, and farmers in general, know the quality of their products and in so doing create a market for them. This does not encourage them to breed a better quality of animals, since they take part in these
public shows simply to sell and advertise their stock. When you go to the rural fair, the district exhibition, you meet there the general farmer with all kinds of produce, who in a real spirit of rivalry tries to show that he can do better than his neighbour. His interest is not strictly commercial, nor his aim money-making. It is rather a matter of pride. He wants to show that he can do better than his neighbours, and to earn the reputation of being a model farmer in his district. I believe that this is the spirit which should be encouraged in the farmers; we should urge them to attempt to surpass each other. We would thus attain the aim of these exhibitions, which is to better the breed of our herds and poultry generally. With the present system, it is only the largest regional exhibitions which are subsidised and the people who win the prizes are not those needing encouragement. This is why the motion of the hon. member from Vercheres is doubly praiseworthy, since it tends to encourage those who really need encouragement and in bettering the agricultural output, would thus add to the asset of our country.
We have in our rural districts several kinds of agricultural exhibitions. These exhibitions count usually upon the generosity of members of Parliament, municipal councillors, priests, and they are practically dependent upon charity for the recognition of the work exhibited. To mention but a few, besides the big country fair, we have that of the farmers' gardens, in which the competitors are often young .boys or children who work a small plot of land, or who raise a few chickens or animals, hoping to win prizes furnished by generous doners in the parish. These youths, rather than farmers on a large scale, deserve to be encouraged. From their earliest years they work on the farm and try to improve their parents' stock, thus learning how to carry on this industry when they will he working for themselves. These youths will to-morrow he the men at the head of the agricultural industry, and nothing is being done to encourage them except through the friendly interest of those about them. There are exhibitions of this kind in all the parishes of our counties. We have exhibitions of domestic produce which depend also upon the goodwill of the people of the locality. Under these circumstances, I am tempted to go further than the hon. member from Vercheres, and to

ask the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) not to limit his patronage to the large breeders of poultry and cattle, but to bring its benefits within range of all the agricultural exhibitions, in giving them, for instance, a percentage of the sum which their management offer as prizes, the amount could be fixed at 25, 30 or even 50 per cent. This would not cost the country much, would help to maintain these exhibition concerns, and would have the double advantage of giving more prizes to the exhibitors and of fostering the increased agricultural production, so necessary for the payment of our indebtedness, thus contributing to the general welfare of the country.
I understand that our friends from the West, who have immense herds and numerous horses for breeding purposes on a large scale, are not very enthusiastic over the motion of the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres, for this motion might result in decreasing, to the benefit of the great mass of farmers, the subsidies from the hon. Minister of Agriculture and in diverting perhaps a large part of what they now obtain. I noticed, the other day, when the Estimates of Agriculture were under discussion, that nearly one half of these Estimates went to the encouragement of breeding and the care of our herds. There was a special item of one million dollars for breeding; there was an item of nearly one million dollars towards maintaining the health of the herds; all this, Mr. Speaker, in the interest of the large breeders; but the poor farmer, who has but twenty-five or thirty head of cattle, who has but eight or ten horses, who has but a more or less modest poultry-yard, derives but little benefit from these large subsidies. I believe that if the motion of the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres were adopted the mass of farmers would be largely benefited thereby and I therefore am very happy to support it.

Mr. Speaker, if this resolution passes, every fall fair and many school fairs in Ontario will also get this grant. The resolution states that if any fair contributes $500 toward prizes, the Government shall make a grant of two-thirds. In this way it would pay the management of every fair to add a couple of hundred dollars or whatever was necessary to reach the minimum amount of $500 and if they received a grant of two-thirds of that amount, that would mean

that they would get $333 or in other words, that they would have to pay really only about $167. Therefore, it would be good financing for the management of every fair to do this in order to get the two-thirds grant.
While I believe that every encouragement should be given to these autumn fairs and to the production and improvement of stock of every kind, when municipal councils and provincial governments are making grants, there is too much of a duplication. During the past two years the present Government has been duplicating too much of the work of provincial governments, and I cannot see the benefit of that. Why should we take money, which the people in each and every province have to pay into the Dominion treasury, and hand it over to the different provinces and municipalities? Such action is all right when the work is on a broad scale such as that of our experimental farms; but if we are going to contribute to local fairs, we might as well begin to contribute to township fairs and to do township work, and if we did that I believe we would be making a mistake. No man in this House is more anxious than I am to promote agriculture in every way, but I do not think this is a wise step to take towards that end. If I interpret the resolution aright, there is no doubt that every fair in Ontario will benefit, but I understand that is not the intention of the mover of the resolution.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? What I mean by my resolution is that there should be only one grant for each riding.

That would create rivalry and do harm in a constituency where there were two or three fairs. Why should the people of the Dominion of Canada be asked to contribute to one fair which is picked out and not to another? In my constituency I do not know which of the three fairs is the best; some years, one is better than the others. I think it would be unfair to ask the people belonging to one fair to subscribe towards a grant for another fair in the same constituency. I agree with the hon. member that it probably would be better if there was only one fair in each constituency; in many cases there are probably too many, but at the present time in many constituencies there are two or three fairs, and it would be very unfair to say that one fair in a particular constituency will get the grant and the other two or three will not get it.

There is one
agricultural society-

speechtext: Order. The hon. member's last question turned out to be an assertion of his own. I point out that when he closes the debate, he will have ample opportunity to reply.

The resolution says "fall
fairs." They are all fairs in Ontario, and, therefore, I cannot see how the grant could be honestly given to one and not to another.

Mr. Speaker, in what has been said by all the members of the House, there is a great deal with which I am in accord. If the Government could alford the money, the grant might benefit certain people who show cattle, pigs and chickens at country fairs, and it might, as the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) said, encourage competition, although that has not been my experience to a great extent. I might suggest that a way in which the Government could easily encourage agriculture in this country more than by making grants to country fairs, would be by reducing the cost of transportation. For fear that the minister might think that everybody in this House was, at the present time at least, in favour of granting moneys to country fairs, I just take the opportunity to say that I think the country will worry along this year and perhaps next year without any additional grant to country fairs put into his Estimates, and I hope that he will not attempt to add that expense to his Estimates.

Mr. Speaker, while I agree that everything possible should be done to assist in the development of agriculture and also in the improvement of our flocks and herds in this country, I cannot see any virtue in this resolution along that line. As pointed out by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson), in Saskatchewan, country fairs or agricultural shows receive assistance from our provincial Department of Agriculture. That department is presided ever by a practical farmer who, I am sure, will see to it that everything of a provincial nature is done for the advancement of agriculture in that province. The hon. gentleman who moved this resolution has said that he wants it to apply just to one fair in each constituency. In the constituency of Last Mountain there are twelve
of these small fairs, and I would not like to be the one to select the particular fair which was to receive this grant. For that reason, and for the one big reason that I think this Parliament and Government should practise the strictest economy in all lines of expenditure, I am opposed to the resolution.

speakeroldname: Hon. S. F. TOLMIE (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to what hon. gentlemen have had to say with regard to the granting of money by the Federal Government to small exhibitions. In the Department of Agriculture, we have adopted a policy of making grants to interprovincial and national shows rather than to the smaller shows. We . have always felt that the small show comes within the purview of provincial Governments which are well able to take care of such shows. We feel that the provincial Governments should do their share, and that the work of handling the small shows belongs more to a Provincial Government than to a Federal Government. I do not want for a moment to speak in any slighting way of the work that these small shows are doing. They are rendering a very valuable service to agriculture and act as feeders to the bigger shows. We are giving aid to agriculture and particularly to the livestock industry in many ways. Amongst such policies might be mentioned :
Federal aid to horse breeding-.. .. $125,000 Distribution of pure bred sires..	155,000
Record of performance for dairy
cattle	 25,000
District field work re cattle.. ..	45,000
District field work re sheep.. ..	35,000
District field work re poultry. ..." 60,000 District field work re hogs.. ..	20,000
Total	I .. $465,000
This does not by any means exhaust the list of our activities in connection . with the livestock industry. Our other work includes the co-operative marketing of livestock, wool and eggs, the replacement of scrub sires, the organization of committees to promote better business methods in production and marketing, assistance to boys' and girls' clubs in connection with the production and marketing of hogs, the supervision and operation of stock yards and stock yard exchanges, the issue of daily, weekly and yearly livestock market reports, the inspection and grading of wool and eggs, financial aid in connection with the registration of live-

stock, and the presentation of educational livestock exhibits at our different exhibitions.
Comparing the small fair with the big fair, one of the previous speakers said that the big fair did not fill a valuable niche in the progress of our livestock industry, or sonfething to that effect. Now a breeder of pure-bred cattle in a back country district may successfully exhibit his stock at a local fair and win year after year, until finally he begins to think that he has quite a good line of cattle or some other line of livestock, but when he goes.to the big fair that is assisted by the Federal Government, and where big enough prizes are offered to enable the poor man to take his stock, he meets with real competition and soon finds out that to win there he must have very much better cattle than he possesses. He is able to see a very large display of livestock there, and purchase such animals as he might think necessary to improve his herds. It is not always the big man that wins at the-big show, as has been stated. In fact, these shows have been the means of bringing out young breeders who are anxious to produce cattle of good quality, but who did not know how good their cattle were until they took them to the big shows and competed with the big breeders. There are many cases where the success of these men with their cattle at these exhibitions has been the foundation of very much greater successes in subsequent years.
I notice also that some of the bigger shows were criticised for having attractions at the show. To operate a show successfully you must have the attendance through the gate, or some other source of revenue. An exhibition that is run for a week or ten days must have a varying programme to attract all kinds of people. A great many people who go to shows are not very much interested in some of the agricultural lines, but a show in Toronto or some other big city draws people by attractions of different kinds, and the managers must take advantage of the general population that patronize these shows by having such attractions as will bring them through the gates. Once having received that money through the gates, they are able to distribute it among the stock breeders and other lines of exhibitors, to the advantage of agriculture in the long run. I have pointed out the policy of the Government in this connection. We feel we have drawn the line at a safe figure. It is our intention to assist

the inter-provincial and national show's, leaving the smaller shows to be taken care of by thep rovinces, which I think, are well able to undertake that responsibility. On these grounds, I must oppose the resolution.

Of course, it is not my intention to press this resolution to a vote, though I felt when I brought it in, that it would be of such help to the farmers that the minister would probably accept it, and I still hope that after he has had time to investigate the matter properly, if I come back next year with the same resolution, he will agree to it.
I will now try and answer some of the objections that have been made by some hon. members. My hon. friend from Fron-tenac (Mr. Edwards), who I was very glad to see supported the resolution, raised only one objection. He stated, and the Minister of Agriculture raised the same objection, that the provincial governments should do their share in supporting the local exhibitions. That is true, and if it is the same in other provinces as in the province of Quebec, they do support these local exhibitions. My hon. friend from Fron-tenac stated that he would support my resolution if it was couched in such a way as to provide that the Federal Government would contribute the same amount that the Provincial Government did. I would agree to that, because I believe it would mean the counties would get a larger grant than they would under my resolution. I believe, and I think I can prove, that the Provincial Government grants more to the county and local shows than they would get under this resolution, which provides for only two-thirds of the amount spent in the preceding year. I do not know how it is in Ontario, but in Quebec the Government grants $2 for each member of the agricultural society. In answer to my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson), I may say that there is only one agricultural society in each county in the province of Quebec. We have an agricultural society in the county of Chambly, for instance, and another in the county of Vercheres. There is only one in each county, to which practically all the progressive farmers belong, and as the Provincial Government grants $2 for each member of the society, I think if the suggestion of my hon. friend from Frontenac were followed, these shows would receive more than they would under the resolution now before the House.
I was greatly surprised to hear the speech of my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle.

It has been said very often that the Agrarian party was in favour of class legislation, Well, I think we had proof of that assertion this afternoon. My hon. friend is not in favour of grants to poultry and animal exhibitions, because in the West the farmers grow only grain and care only for that, practically speaking. If my resolution asked for a grant for grain exhibitions, I am sure my hon. friend would support it. He also stated it was an absurdity to think there was only one small exhibition in each rural riding. He probably did not understand that the shows mentioned in my resolution are shows only for domestic animals and poultry. Of course, we have other agricultural fairs in the province of Quebec at which grain and all kinds of cereals, and industrial products, are exhibited, but we have only one fall fair for domestic animals and poultry.
My resolution would not call for such a very large expenditure, Mr. Speaker. According to my calculations it would not amount to more than $108,600, supposing the average expenditure on the previous show to be $900. We are spending this year $19,000,000 for Militia and Defence, Naval Service and Mounted Police; then we have an item of $16,000,000 for miscellaneous. These expenditures, 'I think, might very well be curtailed in order to encourage the farmers in the development of agriculture.
I do not need to explain to my hon. friend from Dufferin (Mr. Best), that in the province of Quebec-I do not know whether it is the same in Ontario, but judging from the hon. gentleman's remarks, I do not suppose it is-there is only one agricultural society for each riding; so that it would not be hard for me to decide which society in my riding should get the grant. My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Tolmie) has given us a statement which, in my opinion, reinforces my resolution. He has said that the attractions which we see at large fairs are necessary in order to bring money to those centres. That is true, and it is exactly why I desire the Minister of Agriculture to grant some money to the purely agricultural shows, which are deficient in the kind of attractions one sees in provincial or regional exhibitions. As I said before Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to press this resolution to a vote, but I trust that the Minister will take into consideration either my suggestion or that of the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) regarding these shows, because I am convinced that what is proposed is in
the interests of the formers of the country. For the moment I desire to withdraw my motion.
Motion withdrawn.

That, .in the opinion of this House, the future fuel supply of Canada should be considered by Parliament, and that a Special Committee of the House of Commons should be forthwith appointed to inquire into all matters pertaining thereto, with power to send for persons, papers and records, to examine witnesses under oath and to report from time to time.
He said: When people begin discussing fall fairs it is a sure indication of the approach of cold weather, so that I take it that this a very opportune time indeed to introduce the resolution which I have placed in the Order Paper relating to the future fuel supply of Canada. Canada's climate requires the consumption of fuel for seven months of the year. Nearly every pleasure and comfort of life which we have in this country is entirely dependent upon fuel. Fuel is one of the three essentials of life, of which the other two are food and clothing. It is not only essential to the comfort and the very existence of our people in their homes, but it is absolutely indispensible to industry. Our country cannot prosper without power. The wheels of industry stand motionless and production ceases if power is not available. Power for our industries generally cannot be obtained without fuel, and Canada cannot have sufficient fuel for her needs without coal. After the interesting and enlightening discussion which took place in this House last week in regard to the natural resources of our country, it is hardly necessary for me to make much reference to the coal supplies of Canada, but I may be permitted briefly to recall to the House a few facts relating thereto. In Canada we have coal in the east and in the west, but none in the central portion of the country, so that the provinces of Ontario and Quebec have to seek elsewhere for their supplies of fuel.

We have "white coal"
in Quebec and Ontario.

Yes. In Nova Scotia and New Brunswick we have large areas of bituminous coal of good quality, while in Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia, there are immense deposits of lignite and bituminous coal and semi-anthracite. I should like to place on Hansard a state-

ment if our coal reserves, actual and probable, in the various provinces of the Dominion. In Nova Scotia the reserves amount to 10,691,000,000 tons of bituminous coal; in New Brunswick, 166,000,000 tons of bituminous coal; in Ontario, although I said we have no coal, we have, at the south of Janies Bay, a deposit which is estimated to contain 27,500,000 tons of lignite; in Manitoba there are 176,000,000 tons of lignite; in Saskatchewan, 65,793,000,000 tons of lignite; in Alberta, 1,180,000,000,000 all told, of which 845,900,000 tons is semi-anthracite, 217,918,000,000 tons, bituminous coal, and 932,053,000,000 tons of sub-bituminous, with 29,095,000,000 tons of lignite. In British Columbia there are 77,923,000,000 .tons of bituminous, and
5,715,500,000	tons of lignite. In the Yukon there are 275,000,000 tons of bituminous, and 5,159,000,000 tons of lignite, while in the Northwest territories there are 5,280,000,000. And even in the Aretice islands we have immense deposits aggregating 6,600,000,000 tons of bituminous coal.
With such immense quantites of coal in this country, aggregating 71 per cent of all the coal in the British Empire, people who have not much knowledge of the subject may well inquire how any portion of Canada can possibly suffer from a scarcity of coal. Coal is used in this country chiefly for the purposes of domestic heating and power, but it is of no use in these immense deposits unless it can be removed and transported from the mine to the range or furnace in the home, and to the boiler of the factory. From these immense coal deposits, it may be interesting to inquire for a moment, how much is being produced. In 1920, the bituminous coal produced in Canada amounted to 16,623,598 tons. Of this 2,558,174 tons were exported, leaving in this country, of Canadian production, 14,065,784 tons. Perhaps it would be interesting to give the production by provinces. In Nova Scotia, we produced in 1920, 6,395,545 tons, at an average cost of $4.44 per ton; in New Brunswick, 161,164 tons at an average cost of $5.81 per ton; in Saskatchewan, 349,860 tons at an average cost of $2.38 per ton; in Alberta, 6,859,346 tons at an average cost of $4.40 per ton; in British Columbia 2,856,920 tons at an average cost of $5.61; or a total of 16,623,598 tons costing on an average $4.65 per ton.	'
Knowing the production, it may be interesting for us now to learn what is the annual consumption of coal in Canada. In 1920 we consumed 14,065,424 tons of Canadian coal, and 18,742,542 tons of imported [Mr. Steele.l
coal, or a total of 32,807,966 tons, costing at the mines $157,345,552. This shows an increased cost over 1919 of $54,000,000, and an increased consumption as compared with 1910 of about fifty per cent. We may ask where does the balance of our coal come from? We consume only 43 per cent of Canadian coal; where does the other 57 per cent come from? It comes entirely from the United States. In 1920 the imports were, as already given, 18,742,542 tons costing $98,033,598 or an average of $5.32 per ton. We find that our imports are very rapidly increasing. In 1910, as I have already stated* we imported only
10,597,000	tons, of which 3,266,235 tons were anthracite and the balance of 7,331,747 tons bituminous. Last year our imports had increased to 18,742,542 tons. Imports of anthracite in the intervening years had increased to 4,881,313 tons, or almost fifty per cent, while the import of bituminous coal had increased 13,861,229 tons, or eighty-nine per cent over the imports of 1910.
These being the sources of our coal supply, let us look for a moment at the cost of coal to the Canadian people, and after all that is the question that is largely affecting our people to-day. The production of coal at the Canadian mines for 1920 was valued at $76,326,853, of which coal to the value of $18,014,899 was exported coal leaving for home consumption coal to the value of $58,311,954. Of the imported coal, anthracite had a value of $36,773,351, and, bituminous a value of $61,260,247 or a total import value of $98,033,598.
Was that for the year 1920?
Yes.
Did we not import more coal from the United States last year than we produced in Canada all told, that is bituminous and anthracite?

Yes, we imported last
year fifty-seven per cent of our coal and produced only forty-three per cent.

I understood the hon.
gentleman to say we produced 57 per cent.

No we produced 43 per cent. The coal which Canada consumed in 1920 cost at the mines $156,345,552. Let us see how this cost compares with that of previous years. In 1910 the average cost of imported anthracite coal per ton was $4,51. In 1920 the average cost per ton was $7.53. In 1920 the initial cost of

the coal consumed in Canada-that is the cost at the mines-was $116,000,671, more than it was in 1910. But the greater part of that increase, or at least a very large part of it, was due to the great rise in the price of coal between 1919 and 1920. The increased cost in 1920 over 1919 was $59,786,303. If we calculate the increased cost last year on the retail price paid for it, we will find that the Canadian consumers paid in 1920 approximately $140,000,000 more for coal than it cost them in the preceding year, and about $240,000,000 more than it cost them in 1910. This, as I am sure the House will appreciate, is an enormous additional burden laid on the Canadian people for their supply of fuel, a larger burden than is imposed probably for all taxes levied by the federal Parliament.
Let us see how this affects the people? It not only entails a very large direct burden, which amounts to from $50 to $125 per family more than the previous year, upon the people for coal for domestic purposes to enable them to live in comfort, but it adds enormously to the cost of industrial production. Every article produced in Canada last year cost the consumer more owing to the higher price of coal. Many factories in Canada paid out in 1920 from twenty to fifty thousand dollars more for coal than they did the previous year, and many of the larger factories paid out from fifty to two hundred thousand dollars more for coal last year than they did the previous year. So that while our manufacturers and business men may complain of the Business Profits Tax and of the Income Tax, probably the heaviest burden they are bearing to-day-[DOT] if we may call it a tax-is due to the increased cost of their fuel.
May I ask the hon. gentleman if that position still exists to-day?

The condition is not quite so extreme as it was a few months ago, the price of coal having been considerably ' reduced in the last few months. Let me give the House an illustration of how the high price of coal affects our industrial concerns. From the annual report of the Canada Cement company, I take this reference to the coal supply:	[DOT]
For several months the company was unable to secure an adequate supply of coal to keep it running to the required capacity and earnings suffered severely. The president in his address said that the inability to obtain coal was greatly responsible for the smaller business. There was an increase of 540 per cent in coal cost over the year 1914.
That is a reliable ilustration of the increased expense which our industrial plants are subject to on account of the enhanced cost of coal. The higher freight rates and the exchange also add enormously to that cost. In the portion of western Ontario which I represent, three years ago the freight rate on a ton of coal was $2.90; to-day it is $5.29, plus exchange of $1.60, or practically $4 more than three years ago. This means for a town of 4,000 people an additional outlay of from $15,000 to $20,000 per year, most of which goes into the pockets of the United States coal operators and railways. But this is not the only difficulty which our people are experiencing at the present time; there is the additional difficulty in getting their coal at any cost. That there was a real scarcity there is no doubt, but this was partly owing to decreased production and increased demand, not at all to the diminution of our resources. It has been said that for every ten per cent increase in pay granted to the United States coal miners there was a lessening of production to the extent of ten per cent.
We in Ontario-and I am speaking now especially of Ontario-are entirely dependent upon the United States for our fuel, both for our domestic and our industrial needs. The scarcity affects the very foundation of our industrial life, and it seems to me essential that Canada should at once adopt a: policy which will make us independent of any foreign country for our fuel supply and encourage the development of our own coal resources. The scarcity of coal of recent years has been attributed to various causes, principally to labour unrest at the mines, with the tendency among the miners to reduce their output as their wages increased. The lack of cars and motive power on the railways is also a contributing cause. This scarcity of coal will undoubtedly continue for another year at least and will recur at intervals in the future. Let me read an extract from a recent number of the Coal Age, which is generally regarded as a reliable authority on the coal situation in the United States. It says:
The coal companies are figuratively sitting tight and tightening their belts. The spot market is quotable more because of the prices offered by shippers than by business closed. There seems to be a very general feeling- possibly founded on hope-that the buyer is going to stay out of the market until the last minute, and then when he does start to buy the rush will produce another sharp upswing in prices, and that next fall will witness another repetition of serious car shortage.

I believe that that opinion is shared very largely by the coal dealers of this country, based possibly on their experiences of last year, and possibly on their fears regarding next year's supply. What did we find last year? In July coal was being offered retail in western Ontario around $15, and $15.50 a ton; three or four months later it was selling at $22 a ton and almost impossible to be obtained at that price. We all know there was no legitimate reason whatsoever for that substantial increase. But what is supposed to have been the real cause of that sharp advance? It was the scarcity of coal in Canada, especially in Ontario, due to the causes which I have already given. Our people had to have coal, and our dealers felt that they had to pay whatever prices would secure them the coal. While the straight line coal companies were unable to supply our dealers, the independent coal companies, who control a very large percentage of the output in Pennsylvania and the other coal fields of the United States, took advantage of the demands from Ontario and possibly from other parts of Canada also, and would sell coal only when they secured the maximum price offered by any dealer who was urgently in need of coal.
Now, as I have said, that scarcity will return, with all the distressing incidents which we experienced in 1917 and 1918. We all remember those heatless days which were necessarily imposed upon us, when we had to submit to restrictions on the amount of fuel in certain industries, when we were permitted to have only a certain minimum of coal in our cellars, when we were obliged to use bituminous coal instead of anthracite, when we were forced to use wood whenever obtainable, and when even we had to practise the strictest economy in the consumption of gasolene. Those distressing days are sure to return, perhaps not next year or even the following year, but the conditions surrounding our fuel supply are certain to result sooner or later in a recurrence of the 1917 and 1918 inconveniences.
With such abundant resources, and with such urgent need, we should prepare to meet the issue unflinchingly and effectively. And now is the time to do it, not when we are looking for a supply of coal for our furnaces as the cold weather comes on. Now is the time to prepare, not for next winter merely, but for five years from now, when conditions will be more acute, and for ten years from now, when they will be still more acute than they are to-

day. In time of peace prepare for war. In time of plenty prepare for scarcity.
Let me make some further references to the situation in Ontario. One of the substitutes for coal is electric power, and to-day Ontario is using about 1,000,000 horse power of electric energy. It is estimated that each horse power takes the place of about ten tons of coal. Therefore if Ontario were not using that 1,000,000 horse power she would require an additional 10,000,000 tons of coal for her industries. Let us suppose that that was the situation. With the knowledge which we have to-day of transportation conditions on our railways and on the American railways, how could those railways possibly handle that additional
10.000.	000 tons? It would be an absolute impossibility. But some people may say, "Oh, well, we have 1,000,000 horse power of electric energy and we do not need to worry about that." No, we do not need to worry about that. But let us look ahead for another ten years when Canada will require at least 50,000,000 tons of coal instead of 33,000,000 tons as at present; how are we going to provide for that additional
16.000.	000 tons? To-day it requires about
1,000	locomotives and 23,000 freight cars to handle our coal supply, which is one-fifth of all the freight transported by our railways. To handle another 16,000,000 tons would necessitate an increased equipment of about fifty per cent. Are our railways prepared to do that within ten years? Is the Government prepared to increase on our national railways the equipment for coal hauling purposes to the extent of fifty per cent within the next ten years? That is the problem which we have before us if we are going to supply the people of Canada with their necessities in the fuel line fen years from now. Again I say it is time that the Canadian people and this Parliament representing the Canadian people should give serious thought to the problem of our fuel supply in the future.
I have shown that there is an abundance of coal in Canada. Now I come to speak particularly of the needs of Ontario and Quebec, within whose boundaries no coal exists that can be used for commercial purposes. These two provinces, however, are the largest consumers of coal, and sometimes we are almost forced to the belief that in this matter nature seems to have made a mistake. British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia and New, Brunswick have no difficulty in obtaining their supply. Manitoba has had some difficulty; she has suffered in the past, but

with Alberta coal being shipped there in increasing quantities, it would seem that that province has solved its fuel problem.
I would point out that in 1920 Manitoba took 516,198 tons of Alberta bituminous coal, 200,000 tons more than in the previous year. As only 98,629 tons of Alberta coal were consumed in Manitoba in 1916, it is evident that the people of that province are giving the preference to Alberta coal. This is as it should be. The freight rate to Winnipeg on Alberta coal is $5 a ton, and no exchange, a much lower cost than that incurred by the Ontario people when they import American coal. As the Alberta mines have a capacity to produce 12,000,000 tons yearly and as they now produce only about 6,000,000 tons, there is no reason why Saskatchewan and Manitoba need worry about their fuel supply in the near future. The briquetting of Saskatchewan lignites offers another relief, and it may be that these briquettes will in time be commercially available as far east as the upper lakes of Ontario.
As I have said, Ontario and Quebec are the two provinces which are faced by a real fuel problem. Ontario is the one province of the Dominion entirely dependent on the United States supply. Quebec, by water transportation, was prior to the war able to secure Nova Scotia coal as far west as Montreal. While this traffic was arrested during the war, there are indications that it will be resumed and in this way even Quebec may be able to supply
4 p.m. herself with Canadian coal. Ontario alone seems at present completely isolated in respect of her fuel supply -the largest consumer and the most completely cut off from the coal-producing provinces. We consume in Ontario about forty per cent of all the coal used in Canada. The reasons for this are our large population, the gradual exhaustion of. our wood supply, and the extensive and numerous industrial plants in the province. I would like at this stage to read some extracts from a letter which I received from a very prominent retail coal merchant in western Ontario, a director of the Retail Coal Association, in which he outlines the difficulties more clearly than I can. I will read part of his letter. Speaking for the retail coal dealers, he says:
We have learned to our cost that we are entirely at the mercy of the United States wholesaler, both as to the quantity of coal which we can secure, and also as to the quality and price of the product shipped during times of great scarcity. This has been the universal experience of all the coal merchants throughout the country.
The price on Pennsylvania anthracite ranged all the way from $8 to $17 per ton at the mines according as the necessities of the coal merchants might compel him to pay, and if a merchant made a trip to the mines, he found others there ahead of him and the coal was in fact auctioned to the highest bidder.
Moreover, the middlemen were not the only offenders. These prices were actual mine prices from independent mine owners. Ordinary mine run bituminous coal also varied in price during the past season from $3.50 per ton to $12.75 (in extreme cases) per ton at the mines. It was an absolute holdup by the United States operators and the prices demanded from Canadian importers largely fixed the price for the United States citizens themselves, and as a result, a very serious effort was made to have shipments to Canada cut off altogether. You can readily see how absolutely helpless our people would be in such an emergency. This condition, it may be urged, is largely a case of manipulation on the part of the United States operators, but whether this is so or not, the results are exactly the same. Had this winter been a severe one, untold suffering would have undoubtedly followed, as shipments have not been nearly so heavy as in other years. During last fall and summer, when the situation continued so threatening, we endeavoured to get a price on Canadian coal from Alberta, but the best all-rail rate of freight which we could get was $20.50 per ton which, of course, precluded any private individual or company from taking any chances in connection with the undertaking.
Can the hon. member give the price of coal, mine run, in Alberta at that time?

Four dollars and forty
cents at the mine. So that a real problem exists in Ontario. Now, the question comes to,us, how can this problem be met? I admit at once that there is difficulty in finding any satisfactory solution. We must have coal. How are we to get it when we need it, and how can we reduce the quantity consumed, are the two questions which I think we must consider.
Or the question of a substitute.

The question of reducing the quantity consumed would include that of employing substitutes. Undoubtedly, the most promising source of our supply apart from the United States is Nova Scotia, but at present our railways cannot transport coal from that province as cheaply as the railways can carry coal from Pennsylvania, a much shorter distance. What are the possible remedies, then? First, to conserve coal. This is a remedy for many evils, a remedy which the people are slow to take advantage of. But I may be permitted here to suggest some reasons why coal should be conserved, thus limiting as much as possible the amount required.

It is generally assumed that there is enormous waste in the consumption of coal, both for domestic and for industrial purposes. The United States Bureau of Mines say that thirty-five per cent of the coal is wasted up the chimney in the average boiler plant, in some cases much more than that. Even in our homes there is vast waste through the people not having an intelligent understanding of how to fire their furnaces and ranges. A great saving can be effected by a campaign of education among our people along these lines. Another thing which I think might be done to conserve our coal and to reduce the quantity required is to have coal sold by test. Almost everything that we buy or sell nowadays is sold subject to test or according to certain standards; why we should pay the mine owners of Pennsylvania for ash and slate, pay transportation, say, to Ontario, carry that ash and slate into our cellars and from there into our furnaces and then carry it out to the ash heap, is a matter which I cannot understand. I believe the day has come, owing to the scarcity of coal and the efforts of coal miners to sell the whole output without grading it at all, when our Government should protect our people, if possible, by having the coal which is imported in Canada and that which is produced in Canada sold according to test.
Another way and one of the most important ways in which we can reduce the quantity of coal required is by waterpower development. Ontario uses about 1,000,000 horsepower of electrical energy annually, and this is a substitute for about 10,000,000 tons of coal. Therefore, the more electrical energy that we qtilize, the less coal we shall need. With the completion of the Chippawa-Queenston power canal, in Ontario we shall have enough power from hydro-electric sources, it is estimated, to supply practically every plant west of the Trent valley system. The quantity of power required in eastern Ontario and not yet provided for is perhaps comparatively small when compared with that in western Ontario; but possible power development along the St. Lawrence is quite sufficient to meet all needs. While all the power that can be developed there may not be required-
When the hon. member mentions "all needs", does he mean for industrial purposes or for heating purposes?

Only for industrial purposes. I think it is recognized that for heating our homes, electrical energy is not. at all suited. It is estimated that about five horse-power would be required for each individual, and that would make electrical energy for heating very expensive. The surplus electrical energy, which could be developed along the St. Lawrence and which would not be needed for industrial plants, could very well be used in the electrification of our railways. Our railways are using about 25 per cent of the coal which is consumed in this country. Every horsepower of electrical energy which can be used on our railways dispenses with the transportation of about ten tons of coal, and that is a very considerable item in our transportation problem. If we can electrify our railways, we reduce the quantity of coal which will be required and also the quantity of transportation service which we are demanding of our railway system. Another consideration which we must not lose sight of is that, as the days go by and as a greater development takes place, electrical energy will undoubtedly be lowered in price, while the price of coal will, undoubtedly, increase. Therefore, it seems time that we should be giving attention to the substitution of electrical power for coal wherever that is found to be practical or possible. As regards the supply of anthracite in the United States, let me point out that Ontario and Quebec have no other source of anthracite available than the United States. It is estimated by the Geological Survey of that country that their anthracite resources will be exhausted in fifty years, and long before that time we can well understand the people of the United States will insist on their anthracite coal being reserved for their own purposes, and probably export will be prohibited. Another possible means of reducing the quantity of coal required is by adopting central heating plants. While I am not prepared to say very much about that at the present time, on enquiry T find that engineers estimate that, by the adoption of central heating plants in the centres of population, the cost of heating our homes and business blocks can be reduced by 50 per cent, so that this is a matter that is well worthy of consideration by our larger municipalities. Another remedy, and one which the Government can, perhaps, do much to apply, is the supplying of sufficient cars to ensure that

the people of Canada will have their coal transported from the mines to their homes. It is generally acknowledged that much of the scarcity of recent years has been due to car shortage. I am not familiar enough with all the details of that to be able to explain why there should be a shortage; but undoubtedly there has been a shortage, and if it were possible for the Government and our railways to see that there are always sufficient cars at the mines to get the supply of coal which is demanded for our needs, shipped from the mines, very much would be done to relieve the shortage of next winter, and the time to take that action is in the next three or four months, not next fall. As I have said, 33,000,000 tons of coal were consumed in Canada last year, and that was practically all handled by our railways for a greater or less mileage. When I point out that the total number of tons of freight handled by the Canadian National railways last year was only 27,504,000, that gives an illustration of what a tremendous problem it is for our railways to handle our coal supplies. If the Canadian National railways had done nothing more last year than handle the coal of Canada, they would have handled over 5,000,000 tons of freight more than they handled of all freight on their whole system. The railways consumed 7,400,000 tons of coal in 1919, or 38 per cent of the total; our factories consumed 8,000,000 tons in that year.
I was. going to say a few words as to the substitution of oil for coal, but, perhaps, we are not ready in this country at the present time to think of that. It is a substitute for coal as fuel, but the oil scarcity on this continent is even more acute than the scarcity of coal. It is estimated that within five years from now the United States will be purchasing
500.000.	000 barrels annually from the British Empire. They are to-day importing about 100,000,000 barrels over and above their own production. Their consumption is increasing at the rate of
100.000.	000 barrels a year, so that we can see what a tremendous scarcity there is likely to be on this continent.
None of the remedies, however, which I have suggested, meet the urgency of the immediate future. What is concerning the Ontario people at this moment is their supply of coal for next winter. We need
16.000. 000 tons of coal within the next twelve months. How are we going to get it at a price that will not be too oppressive?
Are we to be forced to contribute another $100,000,000 to American interests, while our mines are idle and our railways incurring a deficit of $70,000,000 a year from lack of traffic; or are we going to take such steps as can be taken to ensure that our people'will get the 16,000,000 tons of coal, and at a price which will be as reasonable as it is possible to obtain the coal at? To my mind, we, as a Parliament, should make every possible effort to see that our people are not overcharged for their fuel supplies, even by American producers, and if it is necessary that the coal should be transported from Nova Scotia to Ontario at the cost of transportation I think our Government railways at least should be utilized for that purpose. If that be impossible, if there is no remedy available, the only thing that remains is that the Ontario people will have to be burdened with this enormous cost of our fuel supply for a few years to come, and the burden will gradually become more oppressive. I would just like to raise my voice at this moment in this House in requesting that this question be given the very best and closest consideration. No problem has ever arisen for which a solution has not been found, and if we cannot find a solution for this one, let it not be said that a solution was not found because we did not make an effort to find it.
I have included in this resolution a request that a special committee of this House be appointed to take this matter into consideration. I think that is a wise request. Let us look into the matter; that is what Parliament is for; let us see what information we can get, so that we may be in a position to advise Parliament as to what steps are possible. Then we may expect that these steps, if such are found, will be taken.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to second the resolution which has just been brought in by my hon. friend from South Perth (Mr. Steele), but before speaking in support of it I feel that not only myself but the House generally should congratulate the hon. member for having brought up this important subject and especially congratulate him for the very great care which he has taken in looking into the subject, and in amassing and putting before the House in such excellent order for the use of hon. members all the information which he has given.

I need say nothing, after the speech of the hon. member, as to the general importance to Canada of this question. I presume that practically the question is this: How far, and to what extent, can we make the supplies of coal which lie more or less at the two extremes of Canada come towards each other with a view to meeting, as far as possible, the requirements of Central Canada? Whatever the interest of the province of Alberta may be in tl?e general question, I think it would be quite true to say that its interest will be greater in regard to the question of how much coal it can sell to the rest of Canada.
I need not say anything to this House, because the information is already in its possession as to the almost unlimited quantities of coal which we ha.ve in that province, nor as to the quality, because we have there all qualities of coal. It is entirely a question, therefore, of the area within which that coal can economically be marketed. In the last few years the market for Alberta coal has been extended through Saskatchewan and Manitoba. We have not yet completely captured the Manitoba market, and many improvements must be made by us in our methods of production, and some improvements in transportation facilities, before that market is entirely ours; but we have proven that our coal can economically compete with Pennsylvania coal in the province of Manitoba, and I think that when we get proper production methods and proper transportation arrangements it will be proven that our coal can more than compete in Manitoba with the Pennslyvania product.
Then we come to the wider question, a question on which I am not going to have the temerity to-day to make any prohesies or to give any promises, and that is whether or not Alberta coal can come further east than Manitoba. We might, however, consider for a moment the factors which would influence such a result. In the first place, the question of the cost of production might well be looked into. It is a significant fact that while most of the fundamental products, grain, for instance, have been reduced in price during the last year, the price for coal has not only stayed up but has even increased. The Dominion Government has assumed and exercised a certain amount of supervision and control over the labour question in the Alberta mines, and that question is an important factor in the cost of production. In fact, the cost of production of Alberta coal, has almost doubled in the last few years. It is now [11t. D. L. Redman. East Calgary],
given at something over $4. The coal itself, as far as the leases are concerned, has practically no value unless it can be sold, so the cost of production is simply the labour and the equipment which brings it forth. A committee of this House could well consider this question, as the Dominion Government has already assumed some control in regard to the question of the cost of labour that is involved in the production of our coal.
But the more important matter, in fact the real question in considering the market which our coal could reach, is the question of transportation. Here again, we find that transportation rates have not gone down this last year, and again we are met by the question of labour. Now whatever may be the relation of market transportation costs generally. I would like to say this:	A
proposal has been made from Alberta in the last two years that during the summer months, when the' freight cars in Alberta and Western Canada are not being used in transporting the grain crop, and when there is not any congestion, when there is, in fact, not sufficient traffic to keep our railroads busy, these cars could be economically used in bringing our coal eastward at a considerably reduced rate as compared with the rate which prevails throughout the rest of the year. I think it has been proven that that can be economically done. It would cheapen the cost of production in that it would give labour all the year around to the miners; it would avoid congestion in the winter time, when the transportation of all products is more difficult, and when the grain is coming eastward. If some such arrangement as this were made, I think it would enable us perhaps to widen our market, and in any event deliver our coal more cheaply throughout the province of Manitoba.
Does my hon. friend mean to say that freight cars used for the transportation of grain can be used economically for the transportation of coal?

Oh yes, we do that out
there. In fact, in Western Canada we use box cars more than any other kind for shipping coal. I have only to add that I think a parliamentary committee would be an excellent organization to consider such a subject as this. I can think of no argument why committees of this House should not consider more subjects than they do.
I think myself, and I think other hon. members agree, that our time is often much
