better spent in getting together in a committee and going to the root of some question, than in making or listening to general remarks in this House on many subjects.
So that, having regard to the importance of the subject, not only to-day but in view of future needs, I would seriously urge that the resolution brought forward to-day by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Steele), be very favourably considered by the Government.	i

I
desire to say just a few words on this urgent and important subject. The whole question has been so well discussed by the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) that there is little left to be said except perhaps from the Ontario viewpoint. The facts are plain, I think, to every hon. member who comes from that province. The question of fuel supply has become one of the most important and one of the gravest of all the problems that confront our people to-day. The situation is this. The wood supply in Ontario, particularly in the older sections of the province, has almost entirely disappeared. Electrical energy has not been developed to such an extent that it may take the place of wood, and as a consequence we are more dependent every day upon the supply of coal we get, not only for our industries, but for our homes as well. The difficulty of obtaining a supply of coal for these purposes is not only increasing, but increasing rapidly. To a large extent, it is true that our industries are in greater need of a steady supply of coal than are private citizens, but, on the other hand, there is an increasing demand for coal for domestic purposes for the reason I have already mentioned, namely, the depletion of our wood supply. Coal is being used to-day not only in our urban centres, but by the farmers as well. The farmers throughout the western part of Ontario are using coal to a large extent, and therefore a proper supply has become essential for three purposes: first, for use in the homes; secondly, for the purposes of industry; and thirdly, for lighting a great many cities and towns throughout the country. We are in an unfortunate position as a province in not having within our borders any natural resources such as are found in the East and in the West. That is our difficulty.
This is not the first time that this matter has been brought up in this House. Last session, the hon. member for Maisoneuve (Mr. Lemieux) brought it up some time in the month of June, and in reply to birn at that time the Prime Minister of the day
(Sir Robert Borden) remarked that the question was a most important one which we must look pretty squarely in the face. He declared that the then Government or future governments would have to look this matter squarely in the face. I do not know what the right hon. gentleman meant by that statement, but I do feel that the present Government and past governments as well have dallied with this question too long, and the situation has become too urgent and acute for us to leave it in its present state. I think, therefore, that the motion of the hon. member for Perth is most opportune. I am not going to go into details in regard to statistics on the subject. The mover of the resolution has already done that, but the fact remains that we import half as much coal as we produce, and as the late Prime Minister said, the questions seems to be to a large extent one of transportation. Not only from the standpoint of Ontario but from the point of view of the nation as a whole, I would urge the necessity of something being done at the present time in this matter. It is all very well to say that the question of transportation is so large *-and undoubtedly it is-that we are having great trouble in connection therewith at the present time. But as a Parliament trying to serve the needs of the Canadian people, it is incumbent upon us to meet the difficulties that face us, no matter how formidable they may be. It is the duty of this Government, and if the Government fails to shoulder its responsibility in the matter, then it is the duty of Parliament, to find a remedy for this urgent problem.
What is our position? I contend that as a nation-for we claim we are a nation- we are most unfortunately dependent upon others for those things which we should provide for ourselves. We have 71 per cent of the available coal supply in the British Empire, and we have 11 or 12 per cent of the coal production of the world, and yet, in these two great industrial provinces, we are absolutely dependent on our neighbours to the south. The people of Ontario, therefore, and particularly the poorer classes, look not only with misgiving but with positive dread upon the advent of fall and winter. Eight or nine years ago they could buy coal for their homes at a price ranging from $6.00 to $6.50 per ton, but during the last winter we have been paying in Ontario, in the county of Middlesex anyway, as high as $23 and $24 for a ton of anthracite for heating purposes, and as high as $16 per ton for soft coal. Now, this state

of affairs should not be permitted to continue if we want to have a contented and prosperous people in Canada.
If we want peace and happiness, it is desirable that we reduce the cost of living, and this particular problem touches every home in the province of Ontario. But the difficulty lies not only in the question of price, although that is of exceeding importance. When the ordinary labour man has to pay $23 for a ton of coal to warm his little home and give comfort to his family, it is quite a slice out of his wages of, say, $15 or $25 a week, and one or two tons will not heat the ordinary home. As I say, however, the question is not only one of price; there is the prospect of our being absolutely debarred from getting coal at all. Any little difficulty occurring between us and our neighbours to the south would place us in a very hazardous situation. Should their supplies become depleted, as has been pointed out, or should a strike occur across the border, the result might be that these two great provinces would find themselves absolutely without coal for heating or industrial purposes. That is a most undesirable situation, yet it was the situation in which we found ourselves in 1919. I find in the report of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), for the year 1920 a statement in regard to the fuel supply of Canada in that year. That statement says:
Almost immediately after a strike occurred in the bituminous coal fields of the United States. To meet this situation, the export of coal from Canada was prohibited except under license. The Fuel Controller, Mr. C. A. Magrath, did not have an organization to handle the situation, so the Canadian Trade Commission undertook the work, at the request of the Government, under the direction of Mr. Magrath.
It was necessary to immediately ascertain what stocks of coal were in the country, the quantity available on wheels on Canadian railroads, and the minimum requirements of central Canada for the remaining months of the coal year.
After investigation of Canada's needs, Mr. Magrath proceeded ,to Washington and succeeded in inducing the United States authorities to allow Canada a supply of one hundred and twenty-five cars per day, provided that the coal was distributed in accordance with priority ratings, established by the United States Fuel Administration.
The arrangements made were quite satisfactory, although Canada never received the 125 cars per day, as promised: such industries, public utilities and institutions as were short of coal receiving sufficient supplies to keep them operating and heated. Fortunately the strike was settled about the middle of December and anxieties in regard to the coal supply for Canada were greatly relieved. *
I think that the very reading of this extract from the report of the right hon.

gentleman is a sufficient argument to justify the motion made by the hon. member for Perth. These things occurred in 1919; they may occur again this year, and the probability is that we should be absolutely without coal for either our industries or our homes. If such were the case, we should have to go hat in hand to the people of the United States and ask them, in their kindness of heart,-and I admit that they are large hearted-to give the Canadian people a sufficient supply of coal to keep them from freezing during the winter months and to ensure that the wheels of our industries would not be stopped.
These are the facts as I see them, and I do not wish to labour the point. Prices are every year going higher. This is a natienal question. It is not a question as to whether this government can supply the people of Canada with coal at a profit. Coal is an absolute necessity for the people of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. They must have coal, and the Government must get it for them even if the getting of it by the Federal authority involves some expenditure. We do not usually, as a Government, undertake enterprises in oreder to make money out of them. We do not operate our educational systems in order to make money; we do not supply seed grain to the farmers of the West on a money making basis; we do not make grants to agricultural fairs in order to make money for the people of Canada, or rather to put money directly into the treasury; we are operating a system of publicly owned railways and we are certainly not making money out of those. If the public needs of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec-our two most important and most prosperous provinces from an industrial point of view-require that the Government should do something of a concrete nature, the Government should take the matter in hand in some practical way. An adequate supply of coal is an absolute necessity for the preservation and efficient conduct of our industries, and the maintenance of domestic and social life in the province of Ontario-almost to as great an extent indeed as the British navy is necessary to the existence of the British nation. And yet when this vital matter is brought up somebody wants to know whether it is not going to cost money. In my opinion the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) has presented facts which are absolutely beyond question; and even if it does involve an expenditure of public money some method should be pro-

vided whereby coal can be brought from our eastern and western mines to supply the needs of the Canadian people. What does the present situation mean in other ways? We are now paying out some ninety or one hundred million dollars to the Americans for coal. We talk about the adverse balance of trade, and the adverse exchange rate. Well, the Minister of Finance declares that we will be able to meet the indebtedness involved by our present national debt if we will only adopt throughout the country the slogan "Buy in Canada." Very good, here is an opportunity to carry out this slogan. Let us buy Canadian coal for our necessities and avoid the sending out of ninety or one hundred millions of dollars to the American people. Let us spend that money in the purchase of Canadian coal and thus help our own miners and labourers. I am not trying to advance any definite method of settling this problem because I do not know enough about the details of the situation. What I do contend is that we have to make a start somewhere, and I think the - suggestion advanced by the hon. member (Mr. Steele) is a good one. Let a special committee be appointed to deal with this matter; let scientific men be brought before that committee and examined-technical men from the Department of Mines, miners, coal operators, railroad men;-and let us in consultation with them endeavour to reach some solution of this troublesome problem. I have very great pleasure in supporting the motion.

speakeroldname: Mr. FRANCIS HENRY KEEFER (Port Arthur and Kenora) :
speechtext:
I want to join in the compliments which have been extended to the hon. member for South Perth for the labour he has expended in getting the data which he presented to-day and the very able manner in which he supported the motion. I do so with great sincerity knowing what work is involved in the preparation of such data. I think that the request made for a committee is one that should be supported by every member. I would like to join in the statement of the member for Calgary (Mr. Redman) that there is not enough use at present made of hon. members in connection with committee work. Very important subjects come before us that might very well be handled in committee by members of this House. We have seen the benefit of that in connection with the Soldiers' Pension Committee. The members of the House include men who are very able in their different professions or
business callings; and, in my judgment, questions such as these could be better handled by these men getting together and considering them in committee, because of the time they could then devote to the work, than they could be handled by the Government, who from pressure of public affairs have not the time. After giving careful consideration to the subjects brought before them they could make their recommendations to the Government which could act upon them or not as it saw fit; but surely beyond all question some valuable opinions and suggestions might be obtained by adopting such a procedure. I sincerely hope the hon. member will be successful in obtaining a committee to consider the subject dealt with in his resolution.
The hon. member mentioned several possible solutions of the coal problem. To my mind there is only one solution of that problem for Ontario and Quebec and that is to burn Nova Scotia coal. There is no use in talking about bringing western coal to Ontario and Quebec-the source is too far away; the mines are situated eight hundred miles from Winnipeg and from that city it is four hundred miles to the head of the lakes, involving a journey of twelve hundred miles by rail to the lakeside ports. Before the war the freight rate on coal at cost was half a cent per ton per mile. That figure would easily be doubled now, so that the carriage of western coal for a distance of twelve hundred miles to Lake Superior would involve a charge of $12 per ton to start with. With such a handicap as that the carriage of western coal to the East is out of the question. But if we take Nova Scotia coal the situation is entirely different. From the mines of Nova Scotia to tide-water there is practically no rail haul, or a very trifling one. From a conversation I had with the member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. MacKenzie) I ascertained that a few years ago the Nova Scotia coal mines were only producing a small quantity-a little over half a million tons; but last year they mined ten times that former output. It is a strange fact that these mines should be shut down to-day. Why is that? One cannot understand it. Are there no orders, or is there some profiteering going on? What is the reason for the cessation of operations? Let us get at the facts. We know that there is a demand for this coal, and we know the demand is not decreasing in Canada; we
revised Edition.

know that there is plenty of coal in Nova Scotia; let us ascertain why it is not available.
Take, for example, the city of Ottawa. The freight on bituminous coal amounts to $4.85 from the mines.
What mines?

From the mines in Pennsylvania. The nearest mines you can get soft coal from are located from one hundred to one hundred and fifty miles from Buffalo. In some cases, however, the coal comes from as far south as Maryland. After the coal has been brought to the St. Lawrence river it comes in over the Grand Trunk or the Canadian Pacific to Ottawa. By the time it reaches this city the rate amounts to $4.63. On top of that you have to pay the exchange on that American freight, and on the American price of the coal, and there is also a duty of fifty-three cents. So there you have five to six dollars which in part could be saved by using Nova Scotia coal. Now, we had Nova Scotia coal coming up to Montreal for ninety cents a ton and less before the war. While that great struggle was on the boats were all commandeered and the business temporarily dislocated. Prior to the war Nova Scotia coal was much in demand in Boston; I am told that city gets a large proportion of its coal from the Nova Scotia mines. Why cannot that coal come into our lake ports, why cannot it pass Montreal? The freight rate by water is very different from what it is by rail, let me give you an illustration. For years we have been taking coal from the lake Erie ports, carrying it to the head of the lakes for use by the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian Northern railway, at as low a rate as twenty-fice cents a ton, a distance of nine hundred miles. This low rate is feasible because of the return cargoes of wheat- thirty or forty cents was the normal rate on coal, but during the war it rose as high as a dollar. Now, however, freight rates are coming down. If you go up to the lakeside towns you will see immense stock piles of coal annually made by the three railways.
Will the hon. gentleman permit me a question? Can he say what proportion of the coal consumed in Montreal comes from the Maritime Provinces? Does it amount to any large per centage?

I have not the figures for Quebec, but so far as our water-borne

coal in Ontario is concerned, I can give you some information.
That would be waterborne also, would it not?
It would be for Montreal. The water-borne coal brought to Ontario amounts to 4,614,000 tons bituminous-
Coming from where?

I take it that that would practically all come from United States ports. Of that about 1,000,000 tons goes up to the head of the lakes, for the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian Northern railways. Then, 425,000 tons of anthracite is taken to the head of the lakes. The hon. member for South Perth has already giveri the total amount of coal coming in by rail and water; I need not repeat them. But the point I want to make is this: You can bring that coal from Nova Scotia up to Montreal for from fifty to ninety cents a ton. You can take coal from the Erie ports to the head of the lakes for forty cents a ton. Now, you have four or five dollars to play on. How is it that- we cannot get that Nova Scotia coal anywhere in Ontario for at least a maximum freight of somewhere about a couple of dollars? One of the difficulties, of course, to-day is that these coal boats have to break bulk. That coal has to be elevated at Montreal and then reloaded in the smaller ships. I think that nearly every member of this House knows my views on this question of transportation. The solution is to allow those coal boats to come up through the St. Lawrence route as deepened and enlarged. When they can sail up to any port on lake Ontario and deliver their coal and thus be not far from any towns in the interior of Ontario, then you will get cheaper coal; but I doubt if you will get it until then.
When we have as a competitor a freight rate by rail for 150 miles that costs us practically three or four dollars a ton as well as the duty, there must be a solution of the problem of bringing this Nova Scotia coal to Ontario points, but it cannot, as suggested, be by rail. The distance is too great and you cannot get away from the per ton cost per mile on a railway.
This country has yet to awaken to what it is losing every year by not improving its water-borne transportation through the St. Lawrence. Our people do not yet realize what this means. The best minds in the United States have realized it, and

they have made the statement-which I am perfectly certain is true-that it would pay these two countries to build that canal and scrap it every year, throw away the capital cost because that is what we are expending as wasted for lack of that water-borne traffic in relation to various commodities. Of course, we are only touching coal to-day.
Now, we should quickly prepare to get some coal in. Our Canadian mercantile marine ships are built as bulk carriers, and some of them adapted to the size of the St. Lawrence canals, and to-day they may be looking for cargoes. It would be well to have this question considered in that way. There are other existing types of boats that could carry coal up through those existing canals to the Great Lakes. When you once are able to send coal right through you would have return cargoes of grain and other products of the West, and a low freight established. Few of us have any conception of the number of ships that are occupied all the year round bringing coal up to the head of the lakes from lake Erie ports even under present conditions.
Might I ask my hon. friend a question? What cargo of coal can be carried through the present St. Lawrence locks?
Their present limit is 14 feet 6 inches draft. The Welland canal is- being built to a draft of 25 feet, with 30 feet on the sills.
What would be the cargo capacity of those ships?

With the locks eight hundred feet long a coal cargo boat of about 9,000 tons could be taken through. The present length of boat that is much used on the upper lakes is 500 feet with a draft of 21 to 22 feet.
I was interested in the boats that could go through the present St. Lawrence locks.

There is no reason why coal should not even at present be brought up through the St. Lawrence locks, but as a lesser cargo would have to be carried at almost the same overhead cost the freight per ton will be greater. But even in that manner coal should be brought up at half the cost we are paying for the railway haulage from Pennsylvania. The canal boat that comes through the St. Lawrence is about 300 feet long. I do not know what she will carry in coal, but you
80S
can get the relation in grain. Her grain capacity is about 100,000 bushels. On the other hand, these big 500-foot lake boats will carry from 400,000 to 500,000 bushels of grain or about 8,000 tons of coal. Therefore the smaller boats ought to carry from 1,500 to 2,000 tons of coal, if I am right in my figures.
Would it not be possible for each of these boats to tow two or three barges?

There is no reason in
the world Why the same scheme cannot be adopted as used to prevail in the old Welland canal, when we used to see barges towing two or three schooners behind them. But we are asleep on this question. We are being robbed every day, and it is time the people were awakened, and the only way you can really awaken them is through this House. One of the quickest ways is by means of a committee, just as we had a committee on the question of prices, and so give the matter publicity. There may be some system at work between the coal operators and dealers or others that has held up the price of coal. Why is it today that the Sydney mines are shut down for lack of business? And yet the data produced by the hon. member for South Perth show us that we should be very busy now providing for our fuel supply. I am therefore glad to urge that this matter receive the very careful consideration of the Government and that a committee be appointed to work upon it.
The electrification of the railways need not be taken up just now, but when it is a fact, as we have been told in this House, that out of every dollar of expenditure in operation of our railways twenty cents goes for fuel, and we have any quantity of white coal right alongside these railways running to waste, there is something wrong. We have three railroads practically alongside the St. Lawrence which could be supplied with white coal from that source, and have that quantity of coal that is now regularly and daily going up in smoke, saved for Canadian consumers elsewhere. That in itself would be a saving. That is a question which this committee could thresh out, and I would like to urge that such a committee be appointed immediately.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton and Victoria) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
wish to join other hon. members in paying my tribute of gratitude to the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) for the great care and extensive research which he must

have bestowed upon the very valuable information which he has so clearly placed before the House on this very important subject. Such information is educative at all times, particularly in connection with so important a subject, and we should thank the hon. member for the service he has rendered the country generally and the House of Commons in particular.
Now, it has been abundantly shown that fuel is one of the prim? necessities of our country, and I suppose it may be classed in the same category as food and clothing. When we talk of ourselves as a nation, as an independent entity among the nations of the world, it is desirable that we should be able to live largely within ourselves. I do not mean by that, Sir, that we should not have the fullest possible intercourse with the outside world, but I do mean that we should develop the essentials of life and the essentials of nationhood within our own borders. The people of the British Empire generally know that the basic industries of England and Scotland are coal and steel. These industries have been developed to the fullest possible extent, and the benefits and advantages common to such development have followed. A careful examination of the system of trade in Great Britain will show that Englishmen and Scotchmen are not fond of exporting raw material; they prefer to export the article in a fully manufactured state, and in that way the most is made of every product of the country, in all its stages of production and manufacture. We have coal in abundance in Canada; we have other products such as lumber, iron and steel, and it is of the highest importance that we should follow the example of our brethren in the old land and manufacture and use these products to the best advantage of the Canadian people.
I have spoken about national assets; and this phase of the question has been referred to by the mover of the motion. As a matter of safety first, if you like to put it on that ground, it is important that Canadians should be able to live by what they do in Canada for themselves. Accordingly, it is important that every Canadian citizen should be able to get fuel within Canada and of Canadian production as far as possible. An extraordinary condition exists to-day. The people of Ontario, particularly the western portion of the province, are in dread of cold weather, in dread of winter, because they have not the necessary supply of fuel-and the same condition exists in parts of Quebec. We have in Nova Scotia, 
as I read in the press and as I am told privately, ten thousand artisans out of employment, walking the streets, and alongside of those men are twenty-five or thirty coal mines capable of producing splendid fuel. It seems extraordinary that there should be such a demand for this article, such an abundance of it lying at hand, such a number of men out of employment who would be only too happy to work, and that nothing is done in order to have this coal taken out of the ground, at the same time giving these men employment and satisfying the demands of the people of western Ontario and other parts of the country for the necessary amount of fuel. The only thing necessary, it seems to me, is to find a practicable scheme under which this could be done. The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) pointed out a moment ago that it is not a very difficult thing to get coal to Quebec and Montreal, though it may be difficult to store it and ulti-
5 p.m. mately ship it further west by rail. That would mean, of course, a second handling of the coal, but it seems to me that coal shipped from the Maritime Provinces could be taken to Quebec and Montreal, whence it might be transported over the Government railway, a road designed for the purpose of carrying heavy trains at a small freight rate. If this were done, some if not all the demand of western Ontario for fuel would be met, to say nothing of enabling us to depend largely upon ourselves instead of upon a foreign country for our coal supply.
Now, there is the business end of the matter to be considered. One of the problems of the West is the matter of enabling their grain to find its way to the markets of the world. First, it must get to the Atlantic. During nine months of the year, I think, navigation on the St. Lawrence is open. It is quite feasible that coal should be brought from Nova Scotia to Quebec or Montreal by vessels which could take on wheat for eastern ports as a return cargo. In this way a substantial reduction of the rate even that prevailed before the war in respect to the shipment of coal might be effected. I think, therefore, that if we as a people could go about this matter in earnest, we might be surprised by the beneficial results obtained.
Human nature, as a rule, is somewhat disposed to shrink from new duties and new undertakings; we are inclined to go along in the same old direction and let the other man do the new thing. But it seems to me that this is an opportunity for the Govern-

ment, if we can induce them to do anything at all, to make a start along this line and put something on the right side of the ledger, even if it is a death bed repentance. I would be glad to see them show that they have some sense of national responsibility and move forward in the direction of opening up these channels which are so essential to the proper development and unity of this country. It is a matter of great satisfaction that in Nova Scotia we have practically unlimited supplies of coal. Many years ago, we thought that we had discovered all the coal that was to be discovered; we have a history of coal fields in Nova Scotia, written many years ago by an English gentleman by the name of Brown. Brown's history is still an authority on the question of the mineral wealth, and particularly the coal wealth of Nova Scotia, and if you were to talk about finding coal outside of the sources mentioned in Mr. Brown's record and history, men would shake their heads and say: "There is no use talking; Mr. Brown knew what he did and what he wrote, and you will not find coal except the seams of coal which Mr. Brown discovered." It is, however, a happy development to find that within the last three months there have been struck, within the territory of the Dominion Coal Company, two magnificent coal seams which Mr. Brown knew nothing about. Therefore, coal is being discovered from day to day, and there seems to be no limit at all to the enormous quantities of coal of very excellent quality which we have in Nova Scotia, that is to say, within the Dominion of Canada. When we are talking about national questions, we name provinces simply as a means of designating where the national fortune is; and it is only proper for me, as a Nova Scotian and as an old coal miner, because I worked in the coal mines of Nova Scotia, and I know what it is to mine coal, to cut it and to bring it to the surface, to speak of the coal wealth of Nova Scotia. It does me good, therefore, to talk of this subject if it is to be of any benefit to my brethren of the coal craft in my native province. I hope the day is not far distant when our men will have plenty to do in mining coal, and when a constant, continuous market will be found for it within our own bounds aud outside of the bounds of Canada, so far as that may be necessary. Last year, we produced only 6,500,000 tons of coal in Nova Scotia, and that was done entirely by single-shifting, that is, by men working only one shift a day. There is no trouble in the world,
when pressure is on, to double the shift, and with the openings that we now have in the coal seams, there would be no trouble in converting a production of 6,500,000 tons into twelve or fourteen million tons, if the necessary pressure were put on the production, and if the owners of the coal knew where it was to be sold. In that way, the cost of production would be very materially reduced. Any business man knows that overhead expenses in connection with 6,000,000 tons of coal are pretty much the same as overhead expenses in connection with double that quantity. As the market becomes certain and the quantity to be produced is sure and fixed, so from day to day would the expense of production be lessened and the price of coal accordingly cheapened.
I have much pleasure in again thanking the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) for the service which he has rendered to his country in bringing this matter so forcibly before the House. I trust those of us who will have some responsibility in carrying forward the idea which he proposes, wil not avoid or try to swerve from the duty and responsibility which we have in connection with this matter, and the Government of the day, which is responsible for the general policy of the country so far as government is concerned, should do what lies in its power in order to further the project outlined by my hon. friend.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) says that it is a characteristic of humanity to shrink from things that are difficult. We all know that. I have found, in legislative bodies, rather a larger number of men who shrink from taking up difficult questions. There is a disposition to go along in the ordinary groove; but when one is urged to get out of a groove and undertake something that has not been done before, there is great difficulty in getting a sufficient number to carry that out. I have discovered that in places other than the House of Commons.
What places?

In the city council of Montreal, for example. For that reason, I have great admiration for a man like the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele), who brings before this House something that is rather difficult of solution. The very difficulties make it worth while, and the obstacles in the way are, as the late

Sir James Whitney used to say, "for us to overcome." We all know there are obstacles in the way of providing an ample coal supply for the whole Dominion of Canada; but it is our duty, as men elected to look after the welfare of the people of this country, to find a solution for those difficulties and a means of providing those things that are necessary for a comfortable existence upon the part of our people.
The subject has been covered so fully by the mover and the succeeding speakers that I cannot do very much more than repeat what has been said. But when Canada has, within its borders, more than enough coal to meet all the needs of her people, and then we import $98,000,000 worth from the United States, there is something wrong with our business capacity. Although this coal is at the extremes of the country, the general advantage to Canada of having our people supplied with coal from our own mines is so great that one would think steps would have been taken long ago, at least to ascertain whether a solution of this question is possible. If we can succeed in keeping in this country $98,000,000 that we now send annually to the United States, we shall be contributing to that extent to the prosperity of the people of Canada, and to my mind, that is a very important consideration. A committee, such as is suggested by the hon. member for South Perth, seems to be the only means of solving this problem in an intelligent manner. That committee would have the power to make all investigations and examinations necessary to reach a decision; all the force of Parliament would be behind its findings, and if it is possible for any body in this country to secure the necessary information, it ought to be possible for such a committee as that which is proposed. Therefore, I think the hon. member for Perth South is proceeding along exactly the right lines.
The hon. member for Port Arthur and Kenora (Mr. Keefer) drew attention to the possibilities of providing, at least Ontario and Quebec, with coal from Nova Scotia. I remember the time when, as he said, you would see on the lakes a large steam barge towing two or three barges after it, really making the cargo which that steamer was drawing three or four times as great as if it went alone. I am at a loss to understand why that system could not be repeated in bringing coal from Nova Scotia to Ontario ports. If that should be done, I am quite satisfied that practically

all the grain grown in Ontario that goes out for export could be taken out in the same way. That would reduce the cost both of carrying the grain for the farmer to the markets of the world and of bringing coal to the people of Ontario. That is a system of navigation that prevailed until they got the big whalebacks and those boats of 9,000 and 10,000 tons. Even with the canals we have at the present time on the St. Lawrence river, that plan should give very excellent results.
As to the coal of the West, I think that at least all the western country should be served by Alberta coal. If that were done it would enable many coal mines in Alberta to continue operations throughout the year, instead of shutting down, as they do now, for a considerable period. It would reduce the overhead expenses and mean cheaper coal to all the people of the prairies. I am not proposing any method to stop the importation of coal to the head of the lakes. That might not be a good thing for the railways, but certainly it should be possible, by specially constructed locomotives and cars if necessary, to supply as far east as Winnipeg at least, with Alberta coal. That is done to a considerable degree at the present time, but I think the distribution throughout the western provinces should be more complete.
I noticed by a document which came to my desk to-day, showing the mineral production of Canada, that the amount of peat produced in this country last year was 3,000 tons, at a valuation of $15,000. It seems to me the development of the peat beds of this province might be carried on more effectually and efficiently than has been the case so far. With coal at $6, or $7, or $8 a ton, perhaps it would be impossible for peat to compete, but with coal at $15 a ton peat at $5 a ton ought to be an efficient form of fuel for a considerable distance from the neighbourhood where it is obtained. In central and' eastern Ontario there are large beds of peat, and I think a very large number of the cities and towns, and a considerable portion of our population, might be served with that fuel, which, while not equal to anthracite coal can be, obtained at a lower price and be put on the market in competition with anthracite.
My hon. friend from West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) has said something with which I entirely agree-that it is going to be a question whether we can get fuel at any price. That has been pretty nearly the case in this country for the past few

years, and that situation will be intensified. I therefore think that all the fuel resources that the country possesses should be examined, to see whether it is not possible for Canada to supply its own fuel both for industrial and domestic purposes, and certainly the question of peat should be considered.
As to the conservation of coal, which to my mind is a very important phase of this question, my hon. friend from South Perth (Mr. Steele) has referred to the possibility of erecting- . central heating plants. I have thought for a number of years that that is something that ought to be done, and any pressure that the Government could put upon municipalities in order to have that done should be exerted. In my own city at one time a company was formed to do heating from a central plant. Their proposition was to heat all the houses in one or two or three blocks from one plant. To my mind, that it a very fine idea. They could use butiminous coal for such a purpose: that is always cheaper than anthracite coal, and only about half the quantity would be required. All the ash and dirt connected with heating would be eliminated by such a scheme. Unfortunately, the members of the city council regarded that as a very valuable franchise, and they refused to permit the company to go on with the work. The municipality itself refused to do it as a publicly-owned enterprise, and they refused to let the company do it that was willing to invest its own money. To my mind, that is one of the solutions of our fuel problem. In cities like Toronto, Montreal, Quebec, Hamilton and London that plan would mean a saving of millions of dollars and not only that, but the heating of houses and large buildings under very much better conditions than obtain where individual furnaces are used. I do not know what any committee could do to persuade municipalities to go into that, but perhaps the publicity that would be given to the plan from the work of such a committee as is proposed would have an informative influence upon the members of the various municipal councils, and bring about that method of heating.
I want to say just a word or two in support of what my hon. friend from Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) has said about the development of electrical power on the St. Lawrence river. There is a tremendously valuable power there awaiting development. It is a work that I think the Governments of the United States and Canada might undertake with great advantage in the interest of transportation and the saving of fuel, especially in this country, but also in the United States. If we had had to supply all the manufacturers of Ontario with coal to produce their power during the war, it would not have been possible for us to have secured anything like the results we got from the factories operating during that period. Let us get another million horse power from the St. Lawrence, and if there is a demand for it for industry, let it go there; if there is not a -demand for it for industry, let us run the Grand Trunk railway from Toronto to Montreal with the power so developed. While the initial cost might be very great, the ultimate cost spread over a period of 30 or 40 years would certainly mean a great saving as compared with fuel, because with fuel it is not only its first cost that has to be taken into account, but the transporting of it from point to point, which forms a very large item in the expenses of a railway.
I want to congratulate my hon. friend from South Perth upon bringing this matter up. I hope the Government will see its way to granting him a committee, and I hope that that committee will stay at work session after session until it finds a solution for this very serious domestic and industrial problem with which our country is confronted.
Mr. WILLIAM D. EULER (North Waterloo):	Mr. Speaker, I think it is
m-ost appropriate that the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele), coming as he does from the province of Ontario, should have introduced this resolution. I may say at the outset that I am heartily in favour of it, because as is generally known, we in the province of Ontario and perhaps, in a lesser degree, the people of the province of Quebec, are very seriously handicapped by reason of the fact that we have no deposits of coal in these two provinces. Yet, Sir, I have been somewhat surprised that the discussion has related practically to only one item of fuel, and that is coal, except that my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Hocken) discussed briefly the development of peat beds in the province of Ontario. I read an article a few days ago in one of the Toronto journals, which I am sorry I did not keep,, because it was written in a very convincing manner. It was to the effect that we shall have in Canada, and

in Ontario particularly, other sources of fuel which will be available long before the supply of coal is exhausted. The writer referred to fuel oils which could be developed in this country, not merely from oil wells, but from the oil sands so plentiful in the West. He referred also-and this is perhaps the visionary part of it-to the undoubted possibility of manufacturing fuels by synthetic processes. That may look rather far-fetched to hon. members, and, as I say, it may appear to be somewhat visionary, but I believe there is a good deal to be said for the suggestion. Twenty-five or thirty years ago, if any man had said that the greater part of western Ontario would be supplied with power and light by current generated at Niagara Falls, he would have been considered a dreamer. Yet to-day that dream is true. That, however, is merely by the way.
I desire to refer briefly to one or two statements made by speakers who preceded me, and to make one point in particular, if I can. Most of the members have referred to the fact that the question of a fuel supply for Ontario particularly has to do with transportation. It is admitted, I think, that the western provinces and the extreme eastern provinces, are well supplied with fuel, and there is no serious difficulty so far as they are concerned. It is also admitted that they have enough fuel to supply Ontario and Quebec provided it can be distributed to those provinces at reasonable prices. The matter of transportation is undoubtedly one of the primary difficulties we have to contend with, but it is not the only difficulty in the supplying of fuel from the eastern and western provinces to central Canada. In the United States, from which we in Ontario get all the fuel that we use, both soft and hard coal, the people have at times been in just as serious difficulty as the people of Ontario, and have paid almost as high prices for their coal. They have found it sometimes almost impossible to obtain coal, just as we have found in the western part of Ontario. What is the reason? They have sufficient fuel in the mines of Pennsylvania, and yet the people of certain portions of the United States have suffered almost as severely as we in Ontario who have no coal at all. I remember reading, about a year ago or perhaps a little longer, that the United States Government itself had to pay $22 per ton for soft coal at the seaboard, delivered to United States war vessels, although it was clearly proven that that coal did not cost

the producer more than perhaps $10 or $12 per ton, at the point of delivery. Yet the United States Government, for the maintenance of its warships, was obliged to pay a profit of some $10 or $12 a ton to the producers of the coal. That is the situation I wanted to point out. Private interests have a monopoly of this national necessity and use their power to extract unfair profits.
Even if we can provide for transportation from the Maritime Provinces, and can get coal from that part of the country into Ontario, I think it would be absolutely necessary for the Government of Canada to ensure that the coal deposits themselves should come under Government control. Otherwise, we should have a situation similar to that in the United States. I am free to admit that the United States people may possibly, at all times, be able to obtain coal, while on the other hand, we may at some time not be able to get any from that country, because, while they have treated us generously in the past, nevertheless, self-preservation is the first law of nature, and conditions may easily arise under which the United States might find it necessary to cut off the supply from Ontario. Practically the only reason why I rose was to make this statement, that coincident with the settlement of the problem of transportation must be the settlement of the control of our coal fields, whether in Eastern or in Western Canada. And while it may be a radical thing to say in this House, yet I for one believe that in regard to any of the great natural resources and public utilities of Canada, including such matters as transportation, where the people are dependent for their comfort and prosperity upon them, the Government has a real duty to discharge in seeing to it that these things remain under the control, if not the ownership and operation, of the people themselves.

The afternoon is passing, and it is incumbent upon me to say a word or two in support of the motion of the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele), a close colleague of mine territorially. I consider that his motion deals with a situation of great urgency. I have listened to the many speeches, all of the same tenor, which have been made in support of the motion, and the discussion has been very illuminating. The main value of to-day's discussion to the House, and I believe also to the Government and the country, is the publicity which will be given to the subject matter of the resolution. It is unquestioned that in the departments of government are vast stores of knowledge concerning the natural resources of Canada, but unless there is a discussion of this kind these sources of knowledge lie dormant there and are given no publicity. For that reason I think my hon. friend from South Perth deserves the thanks of the House for bringing this question forward in the way he has. The appointment of a committee is asked for, and it does seem to me that the Government should, upon this subject at least-notwithstanding the criticisms heard now and then that there are too many committees-hearken to the views of hon. gentlemen and, in view of the importance of the subject, grant the committee that is asked. It does not seem to me that there has been anything introduced in the House for a long time that goes as closely to the public needs as the subject dealt with in this resolution. I do not wish to reiterate the arguments showing the deplorable condition to which either Quebec or Ontario may fall as the result of arbitrary action on the part of those across the line who have the control of the fuel supply. It is time, however, that some executive action of a concrete nature should be taken by the Government along the lines of the resolution, and that a special committee of the House should be given the chance not only to try and solve this problem by recommendations, but also to let their work operate as an advertisement to the capital of the world, showing the immense possibilities, as to profit and public benefit, of the utilization of that capital in the development of this industry.

There is no question to my mind but that the Government should consider what its attitude should be in so far as the nationalization of the coal interests of the country are concerned. That matter was the subject of comment in the House on a prior occasion and I believe it is one as to which perhaps the Government has an idea other than nationalization. But I take pleasure in agreeing with what the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) has just stated-that this matter is of such grave moment, being a necessity of the greatest public concern, that I do not think members would be going very far out of their way in asking the Government to seriously consider the question of the nationalization of the coal interests of the country. I know that it looks like a great undertaking to attempt; but nevertheless I think that in ten or twenty years from now, it may be said here that the Government was very supine when it did not devote its best energies to the consideration of the question of the nationalization of the coal industry. The more the fuel supply of the public is kept out of the hands of private enterprise, the freer the Government will be to take measures which will prove of real value to the public at large. Apart from that, the work of the committee might reasonably influence private capital to enter the coal fields of the West and produce. The more coal there is produced, and over produced, the cheaper that fuel will be to the people; and it seems to me that if there was no other reason than that, the committee should be permitted to enter upon a study of this problem. As the hon. member (Mr. Steele) said a short time ago, we may be up against worse conditions next winter than we have experienced during the past three or four years. I do not know what the conditions were in Quebec, but I think the hon. member faithfully portrayed the difficulties, the expenses-yes, the extravagant expenses- and the deep privations to which the people of Ontario have been put during the last few years in connection with this indispensable necessity of life. For that reason the Department of Railways should take into consideration the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Steele) that there should be Canadian cars stationed at the American mines to take coal and land it in Canada. There is no question to my mind but that the Government might reasonably take action along that line, and I commend the hon. gentleman for bringing the suggestion to their attention.
'
I would go even further than that if the conditions in future are to be as bad as they have been in the past. This country has given bonuses for the production of steel, it has given subsidies towards the construction of shipping-many bonuses have been given to aid enterprises which are not as nearly of as great concern as the fuel supply of the people. It might be all right, therefore, to suggest to the Government that they make a survey of the whole field of Western Canada, which is a veritable coal mine, and it might be worth while suggesting that this committee be asked to consider whether the bonus principle should not apply to the production of coal. I do not for a moment see why the question of a bonus for the production, or the over production, of coal should not be considered. I say "over-production" because you cannot produce too much of that necessity of life to satisfy the wants of the people and help to cheapen the price. I leave the matter there, in the hope that the Government will regard this motion not as an academic proposition but as a real problem which confronts this country and awaits solution. I hope the Government will consent to the appointment of a committee and let them get to work, thereby giving publicity to the extent and character of our natural resources. I trust further that our efforts in connection with this matter will lead to the development, either by private effort or by the Government itself, of our coal supply which is, if anything, as great a necessity as our supply of food.

Mr. Speaker, the motion of the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) is very opportune, I think, particularly so in view of the action taken only last week by the Legislature of Alberta. That province, as has been said to-day, is vitally interested in the development of her coal mines, she having such enormous deposits of coal. During the past two or three years she has been devoting her energies very largely to developing those mines, the result being that she has largely captured the Manitoba market which was formerly supplied from the American coal fields. The Hon. Mr. Cote, provincial secretary, speaking only last week in the Alberta Legislature said:
We have increased our total output to 7,000,000 tons, and we have largely captured the Manitoba market, but we cannot hold that market without a struggle, and I am informed that arrangements have been made by American interests for a strong attack in order that they may regain the ground they lost last year.

He added:
It is not the intention of my department to submit quietly.
I am very glad to note that the Alberta Government is not going to submit quietly, because I have always felt that once Canadians have demonstrated that they can supply the market of Manitoba, they should be encouraged in every shape and form to continue that work in order that we may lessen the importation of foreign goods, and thereby balance the difference in trade which is so much against us at the present time.
Hon. Mr. Cote also stated:
I am firmly convinced that we have hit upon the right plan to develop Alberta's coal industry and, incidentally, all of the other, industries of this province that are allied with the coal industry.
That to me is a very important statement, because if there is anything I want to see in Western Canada it is a greater development of our industrial life. As soon as we have that development the agitation which has continued so long, and which has so often threatened to separate Eastern and Western Canada, will very largely cease. Therefore, it is up to us to do what we can to assist Alberta in her work.
Why is it, I said that it is particularly opportune that we should at this time appoint such a committee? Speaking on the same occasion the provincial secretary ' said:
The coal industry of Alberta is capable of great development, and during the coming yeai it is the intention to have the staff of the Industrial Research Commission, for which $38,000 was voted, devote its entire energies to studying the coal problem of the province in every feature from mining to marketing.
What more opportune time for this Government to do something to co-operate to see if we can solve what is probably the biggest problem we have in Canada to-day? Co-operation between this Government and the various provincial governments has been carried on to a rather large extent in the last two or three years with very great success, and I see no reason why we should not continue along those lines.
As an illustration of the result of that co-operation, let me draw your attention Sir, to what this Parliament did on the initiative, if I remember correctly, of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). Some two or three years ago we voted $200,000 for the establishment of a briquetting plant in southern Saskatchewan. It was agreed that we should
co-operate with the provincial governments interested, and the Saskatchewan and Manitoba governments voted $100,000 each, which I think they have since increased, and the total amount now expended is about $600,000. The question was: Can we solve the coal problem of southern Saskatchewan and of Manitoba from the lignite coal of that area? What has the result been? I am going to read-and I make no apologies for doing so-an item which appeared in the Regina Leader only a few days ago, in which it is stated:
The first briquettes produced by the Government briquetting plant at Taylorton, to be tried out in this city, were to be seen burning yesterday in the grate in the Premier's office at the Parliament Buildings. They were part of a sackful from the first output of the plant sent to Premier Martin last week.
. The briquettes are about two inches square and shaped like a piece of children's machine-cut candy. They are very heavy and burn evenly, giving off a powerful heat. The residue is a fine brown ash.
Those who viewed the fire in the Premier's grate estimated that the heat-producing qualities of the briquettes were considerably greater than those of ordinary soft coal burned on the prairies.
The plant expects to place these briquettes on the market this summer.
To me that is exceedingly important. There are two features to be noted. First, is it possible to take this coal and briquette it scientifically and successfully? It is demonstrated that it can be done. Then the next consideration is-will it be a commercial success? I am fully satisfied that within the next month or two that will be fully demonstrated. The fact that by the initiative of this Government and of this Parliament the task of solving this problem in southern Saskatchewan was undertaken, and it is now an assured success. If we can solve one problem in that way why shold not we undertake the bigger problem for the whole Dominion? This particular news item in the Regina Leader would lead the public to believe that the Provincial Government was solely entitled to credit for this particular work, but I am satisfied that that was not the desire of the Premier of Saskatchewan. He has already enough to his credit and does not need to steal credit from anybody else. I wish to express as strongly as I can my appreciation of the course taken by this Government in starting that work and carrying it to such a successful conclusion.
There is no reason why we should not supply the whole Dominion from our own coal deposits. The hon. member for Port Arthur and Kenora (Mr. Keefer) to-day

said that it was quite impossible for us to bring coal from Alberta down to the province of Ontario. " Why," he says, " you have 1,200 miles of a freight haul." For the first time since I have been in this House I have to disagree with my hon. friend-and I think ninety-nine times of a hundred he is right. But what have we been doing? In the city of Regina a great many of us have for years been burning coal brought from Pennsylvania. That means a railway haul of three to five miles to the lake port, then the water haul to the head of the lakes, and again another thousand mile railway haul to Regina. That is, the Americans can sell their coal to us, notwithstanding a rail haul of over 1,200 miles. When it comes down to our doing the same in regard to Ontario it is suggested that we are quite incapable of handling such a proposition. To me a Canadian is just as good as any other man We can do just as well as anybody else, and I am satisfied that if we attack the problem in a true Canadian spirit we can solve it.
Coal from Alberta does carry an enormous freight rate shipped eastward so also does Nova Scotia coal shipped westward. But let me point out that the more freight traffic you have undoubtedly the lower the cost of carrying that freight will be. Carrying only a limited quantity of coal- over our lines as we are doing to-day, naturally the cost is very high indeed, and the very fact that we are carrying such a limited quantity is responsible for our enormous railway deficits. In the United States wherever they have coal-carrying lines those are found to be the most profitable. In fact, it is always profitable to carry coal. We are not doing it. Consequently we are not getting that freight, we are not getting the return that we should get on the freight, and we have operating deficits.
It seems to me that the only thing to do is to make up our minds that we are going to increase the amount of coal traffic on our railways, as a result of the decreased cost of operation due to the greatly increased volume of traffic, the Railway Commission, it seems to me, would he justified in ordering a reduction of the freight rate. Therefore it seems to me that the only thing for us to do is to make up our minds that we are going to tackle this problem seriously, and where we find the other governments, whether of Alberta or of Nova Scotia, ready to co-operate, we should show our willingness to co-operate with them. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker,

I am pleased to support as strongly as I can the wish of the member for South Perth.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I exceedingly regret that I have not been able to hear much of this debate and to get the advantage of the discussion. The subject is one, of course, with which I came closely in contact during the three and one-half years that I was in charge of the Department of the Interior.
The motion of the hon. member (Mr. Steele) calls for the appointment of a committee in the hope that such a committee can contribute something supplementary to the efforts that have been made during the past number of years to bring about conditions under which a larger share of fuel consumed in Canada shall be of Canadian production. The fuel problem of Canada is one of our greatest problems. The very outstanding fact that of the money paid for goods imported into Canada, $80,000,000 is paid for coal alone, and that this coal comes entirely from the United States-a nation which, above all others, enjoys so tremendous a balance of trade as against us-that outstanding fact discloses the question as perhaps one of the most perplexing with which we have to deal.
Western Canada is replete with fuel potentialities, particularly with coal. Alberta has the largest deposits of coal, of course, on this continent-that is to say, of coal of all qualities. Canada itself, though it labours under the disability I have described, is second among the coal-containing countries of the civilized world. Western Canada, then, has its own fuel. The Maritime Provinces also are underlain with fuel. The central provinces, so far as has yet been discovered, are without great coal resources. The fortunate thing is that where coal is wanting, waterpower abounds; in those portions of the Dominion where we lack the asset of the fuel resource in the form of wood or coal, we have it in the form of water-power. But the application of water-power for fuel purposes is a matter of slow development and cannot extend to such a length as will render it in any degree a solution of the fuel problem in the central provinces, for the reason that with the advancement of time and the development of industry the power that may be gathered from the fall of water will be more and more consumed in industries and manufactures. Now, though the

output of Alberta is today the largest of any of the provinces, and though that output has increased very appreciably, particularly in recent years, we do not yet supply Western Canada with fuel, and we cannot hope for some time, I fear, to carry the -fuel of the West, that is, of Alberta, further-at least to any extent worth bothering about-than the head of the lakes. It is a matter solely of the cost of freight; it is a matter of the relation of the cost of the imported coal to the cost of carrying the freight in Canada. We do to-day bring the coal of the East into the province of Quebec-it is even coming into Ontario- and the effort is to bring the Nova Scotia coal as far as possible westward, to occupy as large an area of the Quebec field particularly as can be occupied by that production. That as well is a question of freight, a question of the relation of the cost of carriage of the coal to the cost of the imported competing article. That is the whole problem. You cannot carry coal for nothing. You may make the rate nothing, if you will, but that does not mean you carry it for nothing; it means only that you carry it at the cost of the country, and if you carry it at the cost of the carriage of the commodities of course it comes out of the people. There is a certain inherent cost in the carriage of coal and no amount of bookkeeping is going to reduce it. Consequently the extent to which that relationship is a factor in the area that can be covered by the Canadian production of coal is not alterable by very much that this Parliament can do. We have endeavoured in recent years-and I think there has been very considerable application of the resources of government to the problem; more than is generally understood-to make the production of the lignite of Saskatchewan such that it could withstand exposure to the air and thus be made available for other portions of the West in particular. In that respect we have had a very considerable degree of success. I am glad to note the reference made by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Cowan) to the success that has been achieved there. My information is-and it is very recent indeed from the Lignite Commission-that they are now at the stage where they feel that the element of chance is pretty nearly negligible and that they can be said to have succeeded in actually commercializing the briquetting of coal. They have succeeded in obtaining, and are satisfied with the results obtained from it, the best binder that can be got. They believe it is the
right one, and the only element of chance, if there be any, is in determining whether or not the use of this binder and the methods of its use require such capital and such labour that the cost is really going to be low enough to warrant-to compel, indeed -the distribution of briquettes at least as far as the head of the lakes and generally over the eastern prairie provinces. I do not think they entertain very much doubt, if any at all, that that is going to be the case. They feel that they have made a success of the enterprise that has been entrusted to them, and I think their view in that regard has plenty of material to back it up; I do not think they are wrong.
In Eastern Canada, in Ontario here, the effort has been directed in two ways, one toward the making available of our peat resources, and the other to show that we have coal at least in the farther northern portion of the province. As regards the problem of peat, there, too, considerable success has been attained. A machine has been developed which produces on a large scale, and which they are ready to turn over to a company,-if indeed, they have not already done so-with a view to the production of peat on a purely commercial basis apart from government assistance. It was a matter merely of the development of machinery that could be put down at a cost, and do the work at a cost, that would enable the peat production to compete. That, I think, they have succeeded in doing. When I last inquired, they were working at another machine or a smaller size which they thought might be used successfully and would aid in the production of this article.
The information I have obtained lately is to the effect that in northern Ontario in the rivers leading to Hudson bay, and in one in particular, there are indications that coal exists in such quantities and of such quality that it is likely it will be of use, in the not distant future, for consumption in this p rovince. I cannot give the House very much information, not because there is anything to conceal, but because I have not as yet learned just what is the result of their investigations. I remember well, only a few months ago, arranging for a- special investigation of that question, and from a memorandum which I received just the other day and which I cannot put my hands on at the moment, I gathered the impression that those who started on the investigation had rather more success than they expected. So much for that.

As regards what a committee might do, and as regards the wisdom of this House accepting the resolution of the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele), there is this to be said. A committee could gather together in convenient form the information that now may be found in more or less scattered and inconvenient form. It could be of use in bringing to the attention, particularly of members of the committee and through them of the House, the real factors of the problem and especially of impressing how earnest and, I think, how systematic have been the efforts to solve that problem. If it succeeds in doing that the committee will be well worth while. The scientific board which has been at work for some two or three years has directed its efforts to this question. The committee will be able to gather much information from that board, and the policy which was foreshadowed in the speech from the Throne, and which it is intended to initiate this session will, I hope, enable that board more effectually to do its work and exert its energies in this as well as in other directions.
The hon. member for South Perth has undoubtedly contributed, not only to the interest of the afternoon, but to the usefulness of the day in launching this discussion, and I see no reason why the request he makes in his resolution should not be granted. Indeed, I see considerable reason why it should. I would like a committee of this House to give the assistance to the discussion of this subject in Parliament that they could give by a close and concentrated study of this question, and if they so give their time and energy to it, they will be able to assist very much in the discussions in this House, and the solution of the problem will be advanced. I think that is all that the resolution calls for, and that is the attitude that I have towards it. I understand other hon. members desire to speak and, consequently, it will not be possible to close the debate at this time.
Mr. J. C. DOUGLAS (Cape Breton South and Richmond) moved the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

Before the House adjourns, I should like, if I am permitted, to put a question or offer a suggestion to the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) touching, the Budget. I do not wish to press

him unduly, because I know the embarrassments and difficulties of that; but there are some matters bearing more or less upon something approaching the Budget, which some of us may desire to discuss, and if the Budget were to be delayed, we might find it necessary to deal with them separately. I would not ask my hon. friend for an answer now, but my suggestion is this: that if, when the House meets again after the Easter recess, he is able to give an approximate idea of when the Budget will come down, that will be helpful to the general business of the House. What business will be taken up on Tuesday?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Government will proceed with Estimates. The Department of Labour and the Department of the Interior are prepared to go on.' Should we get further than Estimates, I would intimate the likelihood of proceeding with the oleomargarine resolution and with the Lake of the Woods Control Bill.
At Six o'clock the House adjourned pursuant to rule.
Tuesday, March 29, 1921
